#5728. FDA Panel Largely Pans Trial Data for Myopia Eye Drops

— Atropine slowed progression but clinical meaningfulness, robustness of data questioned

The regulatory status of a low-dose atropine eye drop formulation for myopia remained unresolved following a day-long FDA advisory committee meeting, but closing comments did not bode well for SYD-101.

The Dermatologic and Ophthalmic Drugs Advisory Committee (DODAC) did not vote to recommend for or against approval of the eye drops, but panelists' responses to key questions posed by the FDA suggested the evidence from a phase III trial of SYD-101 did not meet standards for approval.

"Basically, the summary is that, although the clinical trial is positive, it's not a robust outcome that would meet the standard presented to us as the reason for approval by the FDA," said DODAC Acting Chair Michael X. Repka, MD, of the Johns Hopkins Wilmer Eye Institute in Baltimore. "The issue of missing data remains sort of difficult for this committee to manage."

Primary support for the approval application came from the SYD-101-001 randomized trial (also known as the STAR trial) comparing two doses of atropine sulfate ophthalmic solution versus vehicle to slow myopia progression in 852 pediatric patients 3 years or older. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients with myopia progression exceeding 0.75 diopters at 36 months.

The primary analysis showed that 39.5% of patients randomized to the 0.01% solution met the primary endpoint as compared with 49.3% of patients randomized to the control group (P=0.0452). The 0.03% treatment arm did not achieve statistical significance versus the control group.

The difference between the 0.01% arm and vehicle translated into progression slowing of 0.079 diopters per year or a cumulative difference of 0.21 diopters versus control. In a briefing document prepared for the meeting, FDA staff said the difference, though statistically significant, was not clinically meaningful and that the magnitude of benefit decreased over time.

Additionally, primary endpoint data were missing for 26% of patients in the 0.01% treatment arm and 23% of the control group. Sensitivity analyses showed the outcome data were influenced by different assumptions about the statistical impact of missing data.

The staff report also noted that the trial failed to show a significant reduction in axial length, which raised questions about the treatment's potential to alter myopia-related structural changes. Half of the participating centers did not measure axial length, and measurement was not uniform at the centers that did. Additionally, "external evidence from other randomized controlled trials conducted in non-Asian Western populations has generally been unsupportive of the efficacy of 0.01% atropine."

Summarizing the panel's comments regarding the clinical meaningfulness of the differences observed in the trial, Repka said, "The [committee] basically considered the clinical meaningfulness of the observed efficacy profile uncertain, both because of the magnitude, the question of just a shift or delay in myopia progression by the 6-month or 1-year cycle, and also the lack of corroboration on axial length in those centers that were able to perform it. [The committee] would recommend to manufacturers in the future to consider including axial length as a primary or key outcome measure."

The panel also appeared to agree with FDA staff that the published literature did not provide confirmatory evidence, beyond the SYD-101-001 trial, that would rise to the standards necessary for approval.

"When I look at the other studies, they were not as well performed or designed as the [SYD-101-001] study we're discussing," said panelist Timothy G. Murray, MD, of the University of Miami Bascom Palmer Eye Institute. "The size, stratification, and randomization that was done was a plus. The way that the data was looked at is a plus. The other studies fall far below that standard, and therefore, I wouldn't consider that substantial evidence or a standard for approval."

In a separate report for DODAC, representatives of Sydnexis noted that the SYD-101-001 trial was designed with input from the FDA. They emphasized that the trial met the prespecified primary endpoint and that the levels of statistical significance increased in a multiple-adjusted analysis (P=0.0226). Data for the key secondary endpoint also achieved statistical significance for the 0.01% solution versus vehicle (P=0.0002).

Though acknowledging missing data, Sydnexis stated that "missing efficacy data and discontinuations were not meaningfully imbalanced across groups. All prespecified missing-data sensitivity estimates favored SYD-101 0.01%, with treatment estimates generally consistent with the primary result."

DODAC panelists did not dispute the statistical significance of the primary endpoint but rather questioned the robustness and clinical meaningfulness of the results. Murray said the lack of robustness "calls into question our ability to interpret the data further."

Alex Kaizer, PhD, a biostatistician at the University of Colorado Anschutz in Aurora, noted that confidence intervals for efficacy data approached 0%, making the results susceptible to small changes.

"I think what this means to me, with the discussion around the potential clinical significance and the heterogeneity of the patient population, is that it feels like more data is truly needed to understand, especially in younger ages and fast progressors, what the benefit would be," he said.

Acknowledging that the treatment seems promising and is approved elsewhere in the world, Kaizer added, "These borderline results do make it challenging, because if just a few people change their outcome, it could change the result suddenly to a very different discussion than the one we're having today."

Throughout the meeting, several speakers noted that dozens of studies have demonstrated atropine eye drops' efficacy in myopia and that low-dose formulations are available in many nations, but not the U.S. Clinicians in the U.S. can and do prescribe low-dose atropine eye drops, but the medication is available only through compounding pharmacies.

The DODAC meeting had its genesis in a complete response letter the FDA sent to Sydnexis in October 2025.

"The FDA acknowledged in the complete response letter that this primary endpoint was met but stated its view that the data do not support the effectiveness of low-dose atropine in children with myopia," company officials stated in a press release. "No deficiencies were noted related to safety or product quality."

In response, Sydnexis submitted a formal dispute resolution request to the FDA, which subsequently scheduled the DODAC meeting to consider the evidence in separate presentations by FDA staff and speakers representing Sydnexis, including several pediatric ophthalmologists.

The next step is up to the FDA, and no timetable for a decision was announced at the conclusion of the DODAC meeting.

#5727. The Confidence Trap: What a New Survey Reveals About AI and Health Decisions

The Confidence Trap: What a New Survey Reveals About AI and Health Decisions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare remains difficult to navigate. People often must piece together information from providers, benefits, pharmacy, digital tools and care teams while trying to understand costs and what to do next.

Increasingly, they’re turning to consumer AI chatbots for answers. The appeal is understandable: they’re available anytime, respond instantly and can make complex information more digestible.

But healthcare decisions require more than quick answers. The quality of guidance depends on context. General-purpose AI tools typically don't have access to a person's medical history, benefits, costs, care team or broader health circumstances, and they aren't designed to provide clinically governed guidance.

According to a new survey commissioned by MD Live, 37%  of people surveyed turn to AI chatbots for health questions because they're available any time; 31% because they're faster than seeing a doctor; and 30% because AI is reassuring when people are worried about a health concern.

Most people don’t realize how much what they say, or don’t say, impacts the answer they get. The survey findings reveal just how often people reframe questions to elicit a preferred  response, or how much influence these tools have on site-of-care decisions.

Fifty-three percent of respondents admit to rewording questions until an AI tool gives them the answer they were hoping for. Nearly three-quarters leave out relevant medical history when they ask, and this gap can go unnoticed: 22% believe AI factors in their personal medical history even if they’ve never shared it.

The same trust carries over to their children, too, with 71% comfortable relying solely on AI to determine what kind of care their child needs, and 68% to decide whether their child needs care at all.

The behavior is understandable. People often seek reassurance when they're uncertain or worried about a health concern. But in healthcare, reassurance alone isn't always what's needed. Decisions are strongest when they are informed by relevant context, clinical expertise and an understanding of what happens next.

What we’re seeing is a growing number of people making site-of-care decisions with tools that may lack important clinical context. When guidance is generated without a complete understanding of the individual, recommendations may feel personalized while remaining fundamentally generic.

The issue isn't whether AI has a role in healthcare. It does. In fact, AI's capabilities are advancing quickly. The more important question isn’t whether AI can generate an answer. It’s whether that answer reflects the individual’s unique health situation, care needs, benefits, costs, and available care options. Without that context, even sophisticated tools can produce guidance that doesn't reflect a person's real circumstances.

As a result, healthcare organizations may increasingly face a challenge where generic guidance drives highly personal healthcare decisions, with downstream implications for utilization, costs, and patient outcomes.

AI models can prioritize agreeableness in ways that complicate health decisions. A Stanford study published in Science in March 2026 found that large language models endorsed a person's position 49% more often than a human would and affirmed harmful or clearly wrong choices 47% of the time.

That mechanism explains why rewording works so well: the models adjust to please their users. People have learned to reword their questions because the system is built to reward persistence with reassurance, whether that reassurance is warranted.

The impact of this behavior is not theoretical. The survey found that 59% of respondents say they've received AI health information that they later realized didn't fully apply to their personal situation, and 49% acted on it anyway before finding out.

This is also backed by independent research: Oxford researchers, publishing in Nature Medicine in February 2026, ran the largest user study to date on LLMs assisting the public with medical decisions and found that people using AI made no better choices in real triage scenarios than those relying on a search engine or their own judgment.

A separate BMJ Open study from April 2026 audited five popular chatbots across common health topics and rated nearly half of all responses as problematic, while also finding that the tools consistently responded with confidence and certainty.

Studies show that AI’s clinical capabilities are advancing quickly. But healthcare is different from many other consumer use cases. The quality of the response depends not only on the technology itself, but on how well it understands the person behind the question. In healthcare, broadly correct information is not always the same as clinically appropriate guidance. Not to mention, this isn't a fringe behavior. Pew Research found that a quarter of Americans now use AI chatbots to self-diagnose symptoms, and KFF's tracking poll puts overall AI use for health information at 32%, on par with social media.

The consumer need for fast answers and on-demand access is real and isn't going away. The question is how healthcare leaders meet consumers where they are while helping them make informed care decisions.

At MD Live, we believe the future of healthcare AI isn't simply about delivering answers. It's about helping people make informed decisions with appropriate clinical support and a clear path to care when the situation calls for it. People are already using AI to determine where to go for care. The opportunity now is to ensure those decisions are supported by experiences that combine technology with clinical expertise, helping people move from information to informed action.

#5725. Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch

A new analysis from Monash University suggests that low-dose aspirin may be linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia in older adults with certain genetic characteristics. Researchers found that people with a specific genetic profile who took aspirin had a 70 percent lower relative risk of developing dementia, raising the possibility that genetic testing could eventually help identify people who might benefit from preventive treatments.

The findings, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, were based on genetic data from more than 13,500 participants in the landmark ASPREE Trial (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly). Scientists examined whether differences in participants' genes could help explain why aspirin might affect dementia risk differently from one person to another.

Aspirin Linked to 70% Lower Dementia Risk in Certain People

The most striking results involved genes associated with platelet count. Platelets are small components of the blood that help form clots, and researchers wanted to determine whether genetic variations related to platelet levels could influence aspirin's potential effects on dementia.

After assigning participants genetic scores associated with platelet count, the team compared dementia rates among those who received aspirin and those given a placebo.

Among people in the highest 20 percent of platelet count genetic scores, just 1 percent of aspirin users developed dementia, compared with 3.3 percent of participants taking a placebo. That difference translates to approximately a 70 percent lower relative risk of dementia among those receiving aspirin.

However, the apparent benefit was accompanied by a significant safety concern. In the same genetic group, 4.4 percent of aspirin users experienced major bleeding, compared with 2.1 percent of those receiving a placebo.

A Genetic Clue Could Change Dementia Prevention

Lead author Dr. Peter Fransquet, a Research Fellow at Monash's School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said the results suggest that a person's genetic makeup could eventually play an important role in determining which dementia prevention strategies are most appropriate.

"Previous trials found aspirin didn't prevent dementia when everyone was considered together," Dr. Fransquet said.

"Our findings suggest there may be more to the story.

"In people with this particular genetic profile, we saw substantially fewer cases of dementia among those taking aspirin.

"It raises the possibility that genetics could one day help us identify who may benefit from a preventive treatment, rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach."

The possibility of more targeted prevention is especially important as dementia becomes increasingly common. Dementia Australia estimates that approximately 446,500 people in Australia are living with the condition in 2026. That number is expected to exceed one million by 2065.

Blood Platelets Reveal an Unexpected Dementia Connection

Previous research has connected dementia with platelet activation and aggregation, the processes through which platelets become active and stick together. However, scientists have had a less complete understanding of how a person's overall platelet count might relate to dementia.

The new findings point toward platelet biology as a potentially important area of investigation. Notably, the genetic association identified by researchers did not involve the well-established genetic risk factors typically linked to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.

"What's particularly interesting is that the signal wasn't linked to the established genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease and dementia," Dr. Fransquet said.

"Instead, it's pointing us towards platelet biology and gives us a new avenue to investigate."

Why More Research Is Needed Before Taking Aspirin

Although the findings suggest that aspirin could have different effects depending on a person's genes, researchers emphasize that the results must be confirmed before they can guide medical recommendations.

The next step is to investigate whether the association appears in other populations. Scientists would then need to conduct a clinical trial specifically involving people with the genetic profile identified in the analysis.

"We now need to confirm the finding in other studies and ultimately test it in a trial designed specifically for people with this genetic profile.

"People shouldn't start taking aspirin to prevent dementia on the basis of this study without consulting with their doctor, particularly given the increased risk of serious bleeding.

"If it holds up, the fact that aspirin is already cheap and widely available could make personalized dementia prevention a real possibility."

#5724. From Transparency to Defensibility: The Standard Mid–Revenue Cycle AI Requires

From Transparency to Defensibility: The Standard Mid–Revenue Cycle AI Requires" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Written by: Hani Judeh, MD, CMO and CMIO, Accuity Healthcare and Stephanie Smith, MD, Vice President, Clinical Intelligence, Accuity

Healthcare AI is moving from enthusiasm to accountability.

The Health AI Partnership's AI Vendor Disclosure Framework, described in NEJM AI, gives health systems a structured way to evaluate AI vendors across intended use, system performance and compliance, data stewardship, integration, and lifecycle management. That transparency matters — it gives buyers a better way to ask what an AI system actually does before it's purchased and implemented.

For mid–revenue cycle vendors, though, disclosure is only the starting point. The more important question is whether the recommendation can be defended.

That distinction matters because mid–revenue cycle AI doesn't operate at a distance from consequence. It sits inside decisions that affect documentation integrity, coding pathways, reimbursement, denials, payer scrutiny, reviewer burden, and provider trust. A single recommendation may influence whether an opportunity is surfaced, escalated, deprioritized, or acted upon — and hospitals and physicians remain accountable for the decisions they make using vendor AI outputs.

At Accuity, we believe that responsibility requires a higher standard: clinical and coding integrity.

Clinical and coding integrity means an AI-supported recommendation should be clinically meaningful, documentation-supported, coding-relevant, and defensible under review. It should be clear why the recommendation was made, what evidence supports it, what uncertainty remains, and whether the case is appropriate for automation or expert review. That is the difference between AI that can be described and AI that can be defended.

Health systems are operating on thin margins, which means they need automation that stays reliable after launch — not automation that creates new volatility. Missed clinically valid findings become revenue leakage. Unsupported recommendations create rework, denials exposure, and payer clawback risk. Prioritization pathways without monitoring can make work disappear from view while risk quietly accumulates.

Stable automation doesn't happen by accident. It requires evidence standards, decision boundaries, monitoring, change control, and rollback criteria. Governance isn't administrative drag. It's how automation stays reliable as documentation patterns, payer behavior, coding guidance, and client workflows shift over time. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework identifies these same measures as core functions of trustworthy AI systems.¹

This is why mid–revenue cycle automation can't be judged by throughput alone. A clinically plausible finding isn't automatically a coding-supported opportunity. A documentation phrase isn't automatically evidence of an active, reportable, reimbursable condition. The work requires careful translation across medicine, documentation, coding guidance, payer scrutiny, and operational workflow — and that translation cannot be left to automation alone.

Accuity's approach combines physician-led clinical logic development, physician-coder adjudication, governance controls, and downstream appeals management for the cases we touch. Physicians and coders bring different but complementary expertise: physicians contribute clinical context, disease understanding, plausibility assessment, and judgment under uncertainty, while coders bring documentation standards, coding guidance, reimbursement logic, and defensibility discipline. Together, they determine whether an AI-supported opportunity is valid and appropriate for action — giving automation both structure and restraint.

Physician-authored logic defines the clinical intent of the technology. Expert judgment determines when evidence is strong enough to act, when uncertainty should stop automation, and when human review is required. That is the Accuity value proposition: not automation for throughput only, but automation governed by the people who understand the clinical and coding consequences of being wrong.

Lineage is where defensibility becomes real

A vendor AI output doesn't remove accountability. The hospital still has to act and respond to scrutiny. The physician still has to stand behind the clinical record. The coding and revenue cycle teams still have to defend the resulting claim.

That's why evidence lineage matters. A recommendation should be traceable from the output back to the record evidence, diagnosis or procedure, coding rationale, and logic or model version that produced it. Mid–revenue cycle decisions don't rest on isolated words — they depend on source, timing, attribution, clinical context, documentation sufficiency, and coding relevance. Lineage allows reviewers and governance teams to understand where the evidence came from, why it mattered, and whether it was strong enough to support action. It also creates the path for error review, drift detection, recurrence tracking, and logic correction.

Accuity extends that defensibility downstream. For the cases we touch, appeals management connects the original recommendation to the evidence, clinical rationale, coding rationale, and payer-facing defense. That matters because defensibility isn't proven when an AI output is generated — it's proven when the recommendation can withstand denial and audit scrutiny. Without lineage, an AI output is an assertion. With lineage and downstream defense, it becomes part of an operating model that can stand behind the work.

The HAIP framework is an important step toward more disciplined AI evaluation and procurement in healthcare. But in the mid–revenue cycle, transparency is the floor. Clinical and coding integrity is the standard.

Defensible automation means AI-supported work shaped by physician-authored logic, physician-coder judgment, evidence lineage, lifecycle governance, and appeals support for the cases we touch. That's how automation can reduce burden without hiding risk, support efficiency without sacrificing defensibility, and help protect financial stability in an environment where margins are thin and volatility is costly.

The future of mid–revenue cycle AI won't belong to the largest model or the loudest automation claim. It will belong to systems that can be trusted at the point of use. More defensible AI. Not just more confident AI.

Good morning! We’ve got something a little different for you today – an amazing new story from Megan Molteni, and also a peek at the story behind the story.

And speaking of peeks — I’d recommend this new episode of Commons Healthcare, which examines STAT’s investigative prowess and features interviews with Executive Editor Rick Berke and the late, inimitable Helen Branswell.

Heidy Willis was struggling to get pregnant. And after several rounds of failed IVF, she was willing to try anything.

So Willis flew to Albania for a process known as mitochondrial replacement therapy, or MRT. Willis’ genetic material was inserted into another woman’s egg cells. The idea is that the donor’s healthy mitochondria power the embryo into a healthy fetus and, eventually, a baby.

MRT is not legal in the U.S. But medical tourism agencies charge thousands of dollars to connect women to clinics around the world. Many of these companies target women over 40, even though there’s scant evidence the procedure can help unwind age-related infertility.

“You’re paying for the privilege of being a guinea pig,” a John Hopkins bioethicist told STAT’s Megan Molteni.

Megan has spent the last eight months doggedly investigating the companies connecting women to MRT treatments, talking to dozens of patients, employees and researchers. Some of her findings are, quite frankly, shocking. There’s a coda to Willis’s story, for example, that made me gasp out loud.

Set aside some time today or this week to dive into the story. And below, Megan took the time to answer some of my questions about this remarkable piece of journalism.

How did the idea for this story come about?

Back in 2019, I’d reported on the results of a small pilot study of MRT for infertility and since then have continued to cover developments.

In February of this year, I was contacted by a couple in the U.K. who wanted to tell me about an experience they had with a reproductive tourism company called IFG that was marketing MRT as a sort of miracle treatment for age-related infertility. The woman in this couple was a doctor in her 40s and she’d been taken in by the hope that was being offered for her to have a genetically related child of her own, despite there being scant evidence that it improves the odds of pregnancy for older women.

Ultimately, she didn’t go through with MRT because of some bad experiences she had leading up to it. But she was in touch with a number of other women who were actively in the process and she helped me get connected to them to hear more about their stories.

What was the biggest reporting challenge?

Reproductive tourism is the business of breaking procreation into distinct components that can be routed around regulations and assembled at the end to result in a baby. It is, by design, a complex chain of events often facilitated by multiple companies across multiple jurisdictions to circumvent local laws and so is a pretty opaque process.

With MRT, you’re adding even more layers of scientific and legal maneuvering to make it possible. So getting inside required actually going to the places that patients were going, including a clinic in Albania, where the laws are more amenable to technologies like MRT.

What was the most surprising thing you learned?

One of the things that was most surprising was that we were able to get our hands on this long-awaited data from a clinic in Ukraine that had been at one time the most prolific provider of MRT, before the full-scale Russian invasion of 2022.

I had been aware of them for years, thanks to reporting by NPR and this Netflix documentary.

Scientists I know in this space have been awaiting this publication of data, but with the war breaking out, things had gone rather silent. I reached out to their former embryologist, Pavlo Mazur, to ask him what he thought about these commercial clinics offering MRT for age-related infertility, not really expecting to hear back.

Instead, that started months of conversations. He had data he wanted in the world but hadn’t been able to publish, for some reasons that make a lot of sense, and for some others that have to do with biases against science coming out of countries like Ukraine without a long history of evidence-based medicine and well-regulated biomedical research. Their results are the strongest refutation of the idea that MRT can be a silver bullet remedy for age-related infertility.

No matter what happens tomorrow, health care policy could be in for a shakeup. That’s the message from more than two dozen policymakers, lobbyists, and experts STAT’s Daniel Payne spoke with.

Of course, control of Congress will shape what happens next. But some of Daniel’s sources said the anger with the health care status quo runs deep. One health policy consultant said they’re telling insurance leaders that they predict “significant” changes to the fundamentals of American health care, and that they should “be afraid.”

If you prefer your election predictions via video, check out our new “STATus Report”. And if you haven’t yet checked out our midterms page, do it today! Who knows what it will hold after tomorrow!

Did Daniel’s story about the stakes of tomorrow’s election get your heart racing? It turns out, you’re not alone.

As STAT’s Liz Cooney reports, “studies have found a significantly higher chance of arrhythmias in the weeks just before and after elections, and an increased rate of hospitalizations for heart attacks right after voting day.”

The issue is stress. A deluge of news can raise your adrenaline and amp up your sympathetic nervous system, which can in turn alter the heart’s electrical activity. This makes abnormal rhythms more likely in someone already prone to them. Interested to learn about what researchers found when they looked at heart health around the 2020 and 2016 elections? Read more.

Years ago, maternal fetal medicine doctor Elyce Cardonick met two pregnant women, both suffering from ovarian cancer. The women became friends, meeting up with their newborns and comparing wigs after hair loss.

One of those mothers is thriving, alongside her 28-year-old twins. The other didn’t live to see her child turn three.

Why did one die and the other survive? Read this new First Opinion for answers.

Amanda Erickson is a news editor at STAT.

#5722. Upfront TAVR May Be the Way Forward in Moderate Aortic Stenosis, Trial Suggests

— First randomized study to evaluate TAVR versus clinical surveillance in moderate AS

Upfront transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) was more protective against death and heart failure events compared with clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis (AS) with at least one at-risk feature, the randomized PROGRESS trial showed.

At 2 years, a composite endpoint of death from any cause or a heart failure event occurred in 16.7% of patients in the upfront TAVR group versus 23.9% of those in the clinical surveillance group (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93, P=0.02 for superiority), reported Philippe Généreux, MD, of the Gagnon Cardiovascular Institute at Morristown Medical Center in New Jersey, during the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference, hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

In addition, TAVR with the balloon-expandable Sapien 3 platform had a safety event rate of 5.9% at 30 days, which was well under the prespecified 13.7% performance goal, and the bulk of events were hospitalizations for device- or procedure-related complications (5.6%).

The study was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"Moderate AS is not benign, and these patients would benefit from earlier referral to a valve clinic for comprehensive evaluation to establish the optimal management strategy," Généreux concluded. "Rather than waiting for progression to severe AS, PROGRESS supports TAVR for patients with moderate AS and at-risk features."

Importantly, the trial has follow-up planned for 10 years. In the meantime, Généreux said that the PROGRESS trial has already identified the "optimal time" for intervention in AS considering the balance of safety and efficacy.

Among the clinical surveillance patients who started out with moderate AS, 57.4% eventually underwent a delayed aortic valve replacement (AVR) by 24 months. Of these patients, over 80% had progressed to severe AS.

Meanwhile, the TAVR arm showed the "best hemodynamics that we ever saw" with the Sapien valve, Généreux reported, citing the effective orifice areas, mean gradients, and minimal paravalvular leaks achieved. "The future will tell, but I strongly believe based on the data today ... [that] this is the optimal timing of intervention to ensure optimal treatment for a patient given that we can treat a second time."

"This disease progressed faster than [we] expected," he stressed. "You need to follow these patients. You cannot abandon them."

During a press conference, panelist Pinak Shah, MD, of Mass General Brigham in Boston, called the trial a "truly practice-changing study" that "really underscores the importance of close follow-up and the fact that AS is not a benign disease."

The results also suggest a drastic widening of the pool of TAVR candidates.

A large registry study, also by Généreux and colleagues, recently showed that patients with moderate AS outnumber those with severe AS by nearly 2:1, and over a quarter of those with moderate AS in this study progressed to severe AS by 2 years.

Ultimately, Généreux argued for doing away with the dichotomy of moderate versus severe AS altogether and moving towards intervention on "clinically significant" AS instead.

For their trial, the investigators sought participants who were at least 65 years old with moderate AS plus at least one at-risk feature. The majority were recruited from the U.S. (87.1%), with a minority coming from sites in Japan, Australia, the Netherlands, Canada, and Switzerland.

Out of 1,294 patients screened, 744 were randomized 1:1 to transfemoral TAVR or once-yearly clinical surveillance from October 2021 to January 2024. Mean age was 78 years, and 39% were women. The Society of Thoracic Surgery risk score was about 3.0%, and fewer than half of patients were deemed low risk per the heart team. New York Heart Association class III/IV symptoms were observed in about 35% at baseline. The Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) score was about 64 on average.

The top at-risk features that qualified people for the study were valve-related symptoms (96.4%) and diastolic dysfunction (43.8%).

Généreux reported that 91% of enrolled patients had moderate AS in terms of both moderate aortic valve area (AVA) criteria and peak velocity/mean gradients. The mean AVA was 1.2 cm2, the mean gradient was just over 25 mm Hg, and the peak velocity was 3.3 m/s. About one in four people had an elevated aortic valve calcium score.

The effectiveness endpoint was a composite of death (8.4% vs 7.3%, HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.67-1.93) and heart failure events (10.8% vs 19.0%, HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.37-0.81). Of note, a heart failure event had to meet all three criteria: new or worsening heart failure symptoms, two or more objective indications of new or worsening heart failure (physical, laboratory, imaging, and/or invasive findings), and escalation of heart failure treatment.

Altogether, the number needed to treat for benefit at 2 years was 14 in the trial.

Separately, as a standalone endpoint, heart failure hospitalizations were fewer in the TAVR arm (7.4% vs 14.9%, HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.30-0.77). However, the composite of death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization did not statistically give TAVR an edge (17.7% vs 23.3%, P=0.07).

As for health status improvement, the mean KCCQ score was 79.6 points in the TAVR arm at 30 days. The proportion of patients alive with an improvement of 10+ points in KCCQ score at 1 and 2 years favored TAVR (39.0% vs 23.2%, P<0.001).

Généreux noted that when it came to delayed AVR in the control arm of the study, KCCQ scores generally dipped before the delayed procedure, followed by a substantial improvement 30 days later.

The incidence rate of new permanent pacemakers was 13.0% with upfront TAVR versus 10.4% with clinical surveillance.

Of note, limiting wider generalizability, PROGRESS had notable exclusion criteria that barred people with unsuitable anatomy for transfemoral TAVR, significant clinical comorbidities, very low ejection fractions, or prior aortic valve replacement or valvuloplasty, among others.

"Certainly, we have to be very careful with patient selection," commented Shah. "For most, the lifetime management is going to be important ... A lot of these patients are probably going to come back for repeat procedures."

Four big drugmakers paid tens of millions of dollars to proxies to supply lifesaving drugs to Russian government entities as part of a corrupt system that helped keep prices high and limit access for cancer patients and others with serious ailments, The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists reports. Whistleblower reports allege that between 2020 and 2023, Merck (known as MSD outside of the U.S.), Eli Lilly, Novartis, and AstraZeneca paid “excessive” bonuses to a company called R-Pharm and other intermediaries in Russia, even as the middlemen participated in dubious bidding practices or faced scrutiny for alleged bid rigging or anticompetitive conduct.

#5720. Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin

Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Health systems are losing margins they’ve already earned, according to Sumit Kadakia, CEO and co-founder of Midstream Health. The startup bets that artificial intelligence can improve hospital margins by finding money that is already embedded in contracts and transactions.

Midstream Health, an autonomous financial operations platform for health systems, picked up $20 million in series A funding to expand its AI financial platform. The company is expanding across a customer network representing more than $100 billion in annual operating expenses and over 250 hospitals nationwide.

Valtruis led the financing round with continued participation from Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Foundry and CommonSpirit Ventures, bringing Midstream’s total funding to $29.2 million. Fairview Health Services and Keck Medicine of USC are among the newest health systems to join the platform, alongside CommonSpirit Health, Mount Sinai Health System and Houston Methodist.

Midstream says its AI financial platform helps health systems find and recover margin across revenue and cost, strengthening the financial capacity needed to keep investing in care and serving their communities.

"We bring all of a health system’s data together, across pharmacy, supply chain, managed care, revenue and cost, into a single source of truth, and then put AI agents on top of it to find and recover money the system is owed. We call it the 'second financial brain' for a health system," Kadakia said in an interview.

He added, "That’s a lot of technical talk for a pretty shocking problem: hospitals are multibillion-dollar enterprises, and most of them don’t have any form of managerial finance."

With that data foundation in place, Midstream Health's domain-trained agents proactively flag and prioritize cost-saving and margin opportunities such as missed rebates, pricing errors, payer underpayments and policy-driven denials.

Kadakia describes the platform as "an army of agents that runs alongside a health system’s finance and supply chain teams, never sleeps, and is constantly finding and recovering margin."

The company plans to use the fresh funding to expand its product and engineering capabilities, particularly as it moves into new verticals. It also plans to continue formalizing its sales and marketing functions and building a dedicated research function that owns its underlying data connections, Kadakia said.

Health systems are facing a financial sustainability crisis, fighting to protect razor-thin margins. More than 110 rural hospitals have closed over the past 20 years, and another 720—representing roughly a third of all rural hospitals—are at risk of closure. Much of what’s slipping away is money health systems have already earned, buried in their own contracts and spend.

According to Kadakia, one system can have thousands of contracts across supply chain, pharmacy and managed care, each with its own pricing tiers, rebate triggers and amendments. "Nobody has time to check every one against what the system actually buys and pays, so a six-figure rebate can disappear because one form was missed. Meanwhile, most healthcare AI money has gone into the claims fight between hospitals and insurers. Every dollar one side wins, the other side loses, and the total cost of care goes up. Deflationary AI will make care cheaper to deliver, and the most direct way to do that is making sure [that] health systems collect what their contracts already say they’re owed. Margin that stays buried in a contract never reaches patients," he said.

Kadakia says he has a personal perspective on the issue—his father practiced at two rural West Virginia hospitals that have since closed.

"In today's challenging healthcare environment, we have to be thoughtful about how we manage our resources and continually look for opportunities to operate more efficiently," said James Hereford, CEO of Fairview Health Services, in a statement. "By leveraging AI-driven financial operations, we can improve financial performance, allowing us to focus more resources on delivering care to our patients and communities."

CommonSpirit Health, one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S., was an initial investor in Midstream and became one of the first healthcare partners chosen to implement and validate the platform through integration with supply chain operations. After implementation, Midstream's AI agents provided "measurable gains within days, surfacing opportunities like missed rebates and underpayments," according to Daniel Barchi, CommonSpirit Health's chief information officer.

"It is a closed-loop AI system that transforms financial intelligence into real-time action, delivering a data foundation, visibility and execution capability," Barchi said in a statement.

Across its customer base, Midstream claims it has identified more than 1,500 financial recovery opportunities this year, from six-figure rebates buried by a single missed form to systemic payer underpayments. Early Midstream partners are projecting more than 5x ROI this year. The platform is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026, the company claims.

In the near term, Midstream is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026.

"The longer-term piece is what I’m most excited about, because I think this enables a renaissance in value-based care. Value-based care was built on an unstable foundation. To take on risk, a hospital needs a clear view of what care is actually costing it and why, and the systems to give hospitals that view were never built. If we give them that foundation, they can take on more risk, and that’s how you start to deflate the arms race between payers and providers," Kadakia said.

In the current financial environment, health systems need solutions that can improve their financial position quickly, noted Mike Spadafore, managing director of Valtruis. "We’re backing Midstream because it’s built first-of-its-kind infrastructure to turn complex financial data into action. Where enterprise healthcare technology can take years to demonstrate value, Midstream delivers within the quarter," he said.

AI is intensifying an ongoing financial battle between health systems and insurers, and data shows that this AI "arms race" is driving up short-term healthcare costs. The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association estimates hospitals’ AI coding tools added nearly $1 billion in costs over two years, and insurers are answering with AI of their own.

"Patients, employers and taxpayers pay for that arms race. The next decade should be judged by a simpler test: does the technology bring total cost down? That’s the standard we hold ourselves to," Kadakia said.

#5719. Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication

Missing doses of blood pressure medication could significantly reduce its ability to protect against heart attacks, strokes, and other serious cardiovascular problems, according to findings presented at ESC Congress 2026.

An estimated 1.4 billion adults worldwide between the ages of 30 and 79 have high blood pressure (hypertension), a major contributor to illness and death. Although medications that lower blood pressure are proven to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications, approximately half of patients do not take their prescriptions as directed.

"We have evidence that poor adherence to antihypertensive medication is associated with worse outcomes," explained presenter, Miss Qianqian Yang from the University of Oxford, UK. "However, previous data has come from observational studies and could be confounded by other factors. We undertook an analysis of randomized trial data to assess the true impact of adherence on the benefits of antihypertensive treatment."

Major Study Examines the Impact of Missed Blood Pressure Medication

To better understand how consistently taking medication affects its benefits, researchers analyzed individual patient data from 91,339 participants across nine clinical trials. Each trial compared a blood pressure treatment (intervention group) with an alternative approach (comparator group: either placebo or a less-intensive regimen).

The researchers divided participants into two categories based on how closely they followed their prescribed treatment. Those who took at least 80% of their assigned medication were considered to have higher adherence, while those who took less than 80% were placed in the lower adherence group.

Even with the regular monitoring and structured conditions of clinical trials, patients became less consistent about taking their medication as time passed.

"A decline in adherence over time was apparent, even in the structured setting of trials," noted Miss Yang. Overall, 88% of participants met the higher adherence threshold during the first year, but that figure had dropped to just 79% by the fifth year.

Skipping Blood Pressure Pills Reduces Treatment Benefits

The difference in medication adherence was reflected in how much patients' blood pressure improved.

Among participants with higher adherence, systolic blood pressure, the top number in a blood pressure reading, was 5.2 mmHg lower in the intervention group than in the comparator group. For those with lower adherence, the difference was considerably smaller at just 3.0 mmHg.

Researchers then examined whether these differences translated into protection against major cardiovascular problems. The outcomes included strokes, heart attacks (myocardial infarction), ischemic heart disease, and heart failure that resulted in hospitalization or death.

The findings revealed a striking contrast. Among patients who consistently followed their treatment plans, the intervention group experienced an 11% lower incidence of major cardiovascular events compared with the comparator group. However, among patients with lower adherence, there was no statistically significant reduction in these events.

"Notably, our results reinforce the saying that 'drugs don't work in patients who don't take them.' Patients with lower adherence derived little or no cardiovascular benefit, whereas those with higher adherence had greater reductions in blood pressure and prevention of cardiovascular events," said Miss Yang.

Helping Patients Get Lifesaving Heart Protection

The researchers believe that helping people take their medication consistently should become a greater priority in the treatment of high blood pressure. They recommend more routine assessments of medication adherence, along with better patient education and practical strategies to make treatment easier to follow.

Possible approaches include simplifying medication schedules, combining multiple treatments into a single pill, and prescribing longer-acting drugs that can help limit the consequences of an occasional missed dose.

Professor Felix Mahfoud, Chair of the ESC Communication Committee, emphasized that missed medication has received too little attention as a contributor to poorly controlled blood pressure.

"For years, we have neglected non-adherence to medication as a cause for uncontrolled hypertension. Assessment of adherence should become a routine part of hypertension care so patients do not miss out on life-saving benefits. As healthcare providers, we are here to have open, non-judgmental conversations with our patients about any barriers they may have to taking medication, to help improve adherence."

Materials provided by European Society of Cardiology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5718. STAT+: FDA OKs generic HIV prevention shot, widening access for lower-income countries

Ed’s stories explore prescription drug pricing, affordability and access, as well issues surrounding patents, litigation, and legislation. He is also the author of the morning Pharmalittle newsletter and the afternoon Pharmalot newsletter.

After months of anticipation, the Food and Drug Administration gave tentative approval to Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories to make a generic version of a groundbreaking HIV prevention medicine, a key step in widening access for dozens of low- and middle-income countries.

The company, one of the world’s largest generic drugmakers, plans to start shipping the medicine next month as part of an effort propelled, in part, by several global health organizations to ensure the drug becomes available in lower-income countries as quickly as possible. The annual cost per person will be $40, comparable to daily tablets.

Known as lenacapavir, the injectable drug is widely seen as a game-changing tool for eradicating HIV because it offers virtually complete protection against contracting the virus with just one administration every six months. The brand-name version, which is known as Yetzugo in the U.S., is marketed by Gilead Sciences and was approved by the FDA last year.

#5717. Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude

Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Electronic health record company athenahealth is opening up patient health records to outside AI assistants, starting with Anthropic’s Claude, through a new connection designed to give patients personalized answers based on their clinical data.

The new server solution, athenaPatient MCP, uses the Model Context Protocol to connect Claude directly with the athenaOne platform. Patients authenticate using their athenahealth patient portal credentials and decide what information Claude can access, according to the EHR company. Credentials are not shared with Claude.

Paul Brient, athenahealth's chief product and operations officer, said that information is encrypted in transit, patients control what information is shared, and they can revoke access at any time. "Once the connection is established and patients approve what types of data they would like to share, the rest is between Claude and the patient," he told Fierce Healthcare in an interview.

Brient noted that AI can meaningfully reduce complexity and help patients play a more active role in their care. "At its core, this is about helping patients get value from their own healthcare data," he noted.

Athenahealth is committed to responsible AI integration, company executives said.

Patients are turning to generative AI, like Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, to interpret lab results, medication instructions and other medical information. More than a third of U.S. adults (34%) have used AI assistants for health-related purposes, including looking up symptoms to understanding a diagnosis, according to an August Pew Research Center survey. This trend reflects a growing expectation for immediate, conversational health guidance, but also introduces new governance challenges, athenahealth executives noted.

"Claude is the first connection we’ve enabled for athenaPatient MCP, but it's not intended to be the only one," Brient said. "Anthropic has been a strong launch collaborator because of its approach to responsible AI development. But our strategy isn't built around a specific AI model. The AI landscape is moving incredibly quickly, with new models and tools coming to market seemingly every week. We designed athenaPatient MCP with that reality in mind and built it on a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that has become an industry norm for AI interoperability."

Claude Pro and Max users in the U.S. can add the athenaPatient MCP connector within their Claude settings. Patients can then ask Claude questions about their health information using natural language. With a patient’s permission, Claude can reference information such as lab results, medications, vitals, health conditions, diagnostic reports, immunizations, visit history, allergies, procedures and care plans to generate personalized answers based on their clinical data, instead of generic or incomplete information, athenahealth executives said.

"Patients often have questions about their health records between visits, from what a lab result means to what to ask at their next appointment," Syed Mohiuddin, head of healthcare at Anthropic, said in a statement. "athenahealth is giving patients a way to bring their own records into Claude when they choose to, so they can explore those questions and feel more confident and prepared in conversations with their care team."

Athenahealth's EHR is a cloud-based, open platform, Brient noted, and the company's objective is to "create a secure way for patients to use their health information with the AI assistants they choose," he said.

The company plans to expand access to other models, but Brient did not provide any details about additional integrations.

The company built athenaPatient MCP to connect to general-purpose AI assistants rather than build those generative AI capabilities entirely within athenaPatient.

"It's not our job to decide which AI assistant patients should use. Patients are increasingly using AI tools in their daily lives, and I expect that trend to continue. If we've learned anything over the last few years, it's that people will gravitate toward the experiences that work best for them. Healthcare shouldn't be isolated from that reality," Brient said.

"At its core, this is about giving patients access to their health information in the places where they want them—safely, of course. Our patient-facing connector is consistent with our broader interoperability capabilities. Consumers increasingly expect their personal data to integrate into the digital tools they use. Healthcare shouldn't be an exception," he said.

Some providers have raised concerns that as patients increasingly use AI chatbots to interpret health records and lab results, it will drive an uptick in follow-up messages to physicians. Brient noted that giving patients an easier way to connect their health records to AI tools helps patients better understand the information their providers have given them and have more informed questions.

"One of the realities of healthcare is that patients often leave an appointment with more information than they can reasonably absorb in the moment. Lab results often arrive after the patient has seen their doctor. Questions come up after the visit. Medication instructions get forgotten. That's not a criticism of patients or clinicians. It's just reality," he said.

"When patients have a stronger understanding of their healthcare situation, conversations with their care teams tend to be more productive. From the clinician perspective, we were equally focused on what this should not do. We did not want to create additional work for clinicians. A recurring theme across our product strategy is reducing work while improving outcomes. The best healthcare technology helps patients become more engaged without creating more administrative burden for clinicians," Brient noted.

Athenahealth provides EHR software, revenue cycle management and patient engagement solutions to small and independent provider practices. A year ago, the company unveiled new AI features for ambulatory providers as part of a larger upgrade to an "AI-native" athenaOne platform. This summer, the company rolled out more than 80 new AI features for RCM operations on its AI-native athenaOne platform.

Athenahealth executives describe the launch of athenaPatient MCP and the connection to Claude as just the first step, suggesting a broader strategy of allowing patients to use AI tools with their health records.

"The immediate focus is helping patients securely access and understand their health information through the AI assistants they choose to use. Looking further ahead, I think it's reasonable to expect both the number of AI assistants and the capabilities available through them to expand. One of the reasons we're excited about MCP is that it creates a standardized way to provide context to AI systems. Context is what makes AI particularly useful. Without context, AI can provide general information. With context, it can provide a more detailed, personalized set of information and is less likely to lead you astray," Brient said.

Major EHR companies are moving forward with AI integrations to connect patient data with AI tools OpenAI's ChatGPT for Healthcare now integrates with Epic's EHR to enable authorized clinicians to access and summarize patient information from medical records within ChatGPT or directly in supported Epic workflows. That integration can now pull together clinical notes, lab results, medications and specialist documentation, the company said in a blog post.

Oracle’s AI-powered patient portal allows patients to chat directly with their electronic health record using a conversational interface built on OpenAI frontier models.

In healthcare, MCP creates a common framework for connecting AI agents to clinical systems and data.

"I think it's still early, but this is an important trend to watch," Brient said. "One of the challenges with AI is that intelligence without context isn't particularly useful. In healthcare, context must be accurate, permissioned, secure, and current. That's a much harder problem than simply connecting a chat to a data source."

What makes MCP interesting, he noted, is that it provides a framework for connecting AI systems with the context they need while preserving appropriate controls and governance.

"Whether MCP ultimately becomes the interoperability layer for AI in healthcare remains to be seen, but I think the demand for this type of interoperability is only going to increase. Patients and providers are already using AI. The question is whether healthcare data can participate in those experiences safely and effectively," he said, adding, "I feel good about where the industry is headed, and I believe standards like MCP can play an important role in getting us there. But we're still in the early innings, and much work remains. Our goal is straightforward: reduce friction, maintain trust, and help patients and providers benefit from advances in AI without compromising security or control."

#5715. Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think

Even alcohol consumption that many Americans would describe as moderate may carry significant health risks, including a greater likelihood of premature death, disability, cancer, and heart disease. That is the conclusion of a new study published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, a journal published at Rutgers University.

The research, known as the Alcohol Intake and Health Study, was originally commissioned by the U.S. federal government to help shape updated national dietary recommendations. Researchers estimated that people who consume an average of 14 alcoholic drinks per week face a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of dying from alcohol-related causes. By comparison, consuming up to seven drinks weekly was linked to only small increases in risk for most health conditions.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," says lead study author Kevin Shield, Ph.D., an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

How Scientists Measured the Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand the long-term consequences of drinking, Shield and his colleagues in the United States and Canada investigated how alcohol consumption over a lifetime contributes to disease and premature death among Americans.

Medical experts first examined more than 7,200 scientific publications covering illnesses and injuries associated with alcohol. Using this evidence, they estimated the risks for individual health conditions and combined those findings with large national health data sets. Statistical models then allowed the team to calculate how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious health problems or dying prematurely.

The findings provide specific estimates that are missing from the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines. The updated recommendations simply encourage Americans to "limit alcoholic beverages" without identifying a particular consumption threshold. Earlier versions advised men to drink no more than two alcoholic beverages per day and women no more than one.

"While the new U.S. Dietary Guidelines contain a useful 'less-is-best' message, they provide no quantitative framework. Our study was designed to do just that across the drinking spectrum," says study co-author Timothy Naimi, M.D., M.P.H., director of the University of Victoria's Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and an adjunct professor at Boston University.

"It turns out that two drinks per day, which might be considered 'moderate' from a social standpoint, is associated with a substantially elevated risk of a premature death caused by alcohol," explains Naimi.

Moderate Drinking Offers No Significant Overall Health Benefits

The researchers looked beyond the risk of premature death to examine alcohol's connection to a wide range of immediate and long-term health problems. These included cancers (e.g., esophageal, oral, and breast), cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and injuries.

One of the study's most important findings challenges the longstanding belief that consuming small amounts of alcohol can improve health, particularly heart health.

"We did not observe a significant protective effect of alcohol on health at any level of consumption," says Shield. "At low levels, alcohol may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. But when you look across the full range of health outcomes, including cancer and other chronic diseases, those potential benefits are outweighed by the risks even at 7 drinks per week."

In other words, while some studies have suggested that light drinking may benefit certain aspects of cardiovascular health, those possible advantages do not translate into an overall health benefit once alcohol's links to cancer and other diseases are taken into account.

Although the analysis drew on extensive scientific evidence, the researchers emphasize that its estimates describe risks across populations rather than predicting precisely what will happen to any particular person.

Shield says the statistical calculations relied on "the best possible data." However, he cautions that individual circumstances can substantially influence the results.

"However, we can't assume that means one person's individual health risk is the same as what is reported here -- that depends on other factors like lifestyle, genetics, drinking patterns, and other choices that differ person to person."

To estimate alcohol's overall impact, the researchers calculated risks for health conditions already known to be caused by alcohol and combined them into a broader assessment. However, scientists are continuing to investigate additional possible consequences of drinking, including emerging evidence connecting alcohol consumption to pancreatic cancer.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," says Shield.

What the Findings Mean for U.S. Drinking Guidelines

The results suggest that alcohol-related health risks become more pronounced when consumption exceeds one drink per day, regardless of whether the person is male or female. This provides a more specific reference point for people trying to understand how their drinking habits might affect their long-term health.

Rather than suggesting that any particular amount is completely safe, the findings show how risks increase with greater consumption and why drinking less generally reduces exposure to alcohol-related harm.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking," says Shield.

The study has also raised questions about how scientific evidence was incorporated into federal dietary recommendations.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former Associate Administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, offers his perspective on the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the development of national guidance.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Materials provided by Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Brigham and Women's Hospital said in a statement it received notice from the Massachusetts Nurses Association (MNA) on Nov. 1 about an open-ended strike beginning Thursday, Nov. 12 at 7 a.m.

"We deeply value and respect our Brigham nurses and remain committed to reaching a fair and responsible agreement. MGB's rejected offer would have retained the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. "It’s [time for] MGB to return to the table ready to negotiate in good faith to reach a fair agreement that recognizes the value of Brigham nurses and the expertise they offer for the care of some of the region’s most complex patients every day.”

The 4,000-member open-ended strike would be the largest in state history if launched, and follows months of contract negotiations between the health system and the Massachusetts Nurses Association (see that coverage below).

A formal deal has yet to be struck, though the union said it agreed to call off its 10-day strike notice "given the complexity of the agreement and the impact of a potential strike on our nurses and the community." The proposal is being presented to members for a vote, which might yield a new 10-day notice if rejected.

Brigham and Women's Hospital, in a Sunday statement, said its "last, best and final offer ... reflects significant movement on several of the union's priorities while maintaining a responsible approach to supporting nurses, patients and the long-term strength of the hospital."

It added that the offer retains the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The withdrawn notice also saved the hospital from having to implement its contingency staffing plan of hiring temporary nurses.

"We are thankful the MNA has pulled its indefinite strike notice and will allow its members to vote on the hospital's final offer," the hospital said. The union's statement did not specify the timing of that vote.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have voted to authorize an open-ended, 4,000-member strike that could become the largest nurses’ strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association announced the 93% in favor vote that was held Thursday evening. No date has been set yet by the union, which is legally required to give employer Mass General Brigham (MGB) 10 days' notice.

“Brigham nurses have made clear that we are prepared to stay on strike for as long as it takes to win a contract that protects our patients and respects the nurses who care for them,” Kelly Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse and chair of the Brigham and Women’s Hospital MNA Bargaining Committee, said in the union’s announcement. “An open-ended strike is a serious step that will undoubtedly create a healthcare crisis in Massachusetts. Contract negotiations between the sides have been ongoing since last November, with the prior agreement expiring on March 31. In July, the nurses (plus an additional 450 home care clinicians) conducted a one-day awareness strike that was also a record breaker for the state and the first at Brigham and Women’s, a flagship hospital and founding member of the nonprofit system.

Demonstrations have continued in the weeks since, including a rally held earlier this week outside of an MGB-hosted World Medical Innovation Forum, where bargaining members painted a contrast between executives’ conversations with investors on AI and the demands of their clinical workforce.

The hospital, in statements given to press, said “we remain committed to bargaining in good faith and have put forward a fair and responsible proposal that maintains Brigham nurses’ market-leading compensation, preserves meaningful wage growth and competitive benefits, and balances those investments with the long-term financial sustainability of our system,” the hospital said in a statement given to press.

The hospital has previously said it has found agreements with the union on several issues. However, the union has previously said that talks stalled in mid-August and reiterated Thursday that it still is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

MGB is the largest private employer in Massachusetts with roughly 85,000 workers and $22.8 billion in annual revenue, making it among the country’s largest nonprofit health systems. Financial results released last month outlined a $15 million operating income (0.1% operating margin) across nine months of its ongoing fiscal year, up from a $44 million operating loss (-0.3% operating margin), though its nine-month bottom line including nonoperating gains like investment returns was $1.9 billion. Early last year saw the organization undertake the largest layoffs in its history, when it cut about 1,500 workers.

The union has pointed to MGB’s bottom line (nearly $2.4 billion across fiscal 2025), substantial total assets ($35.8 billion) and the compensation of executives (almost $9.2 million for CEO Anne Klibanski, M.D.) in its calls for stronger contracts.

#5712. AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis

An artificial intelligence model called REDMOD can identify extremely subtle changes in pancreatic tissue that may signal cancer long before the disease becomes visible to doctors or conventional imaging technology. According to research published online in the journal Gut, the system can detect early signs of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer.

Researchers believe this technology could help transform pancreatic cancer detection by identifying the disease at a much earlier stage (stage 0), when treatment is more likely to succeed. Instead of receiving a diagnosis after the cancer has progressed to an advanced, potentially terminal stage, patients might have an opportunity to begin treatment while the disease is still treatable.

Although REDMOD outperformed experienced radiologists in the study, more research is necessary before it can be introduced into routine medical care. In particular, the scientists emphasize the need to test the system in patients at high risk, including those experiencing unexplained weight loss or recently diagnosed diabetes.

Why Pancreatic Cancer Is So Difficult to Detect Early

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a low survival rate, largely because it is often discovered only after the disease has advanced. Early pancreatic cancer typically produces few noticeable symptoms, and the changes it causes in pancreatic tissue can be too subtle to detect through standard medical imaging. The cancer can also progress rapidly, making timely diagnosis especially important.

To address these challenges, researchers created an artificial intelligence framework known as Radiomics-based Early Detection MODel (REDMOD). The system analyzes extremely fine patterns in the texture of pancreatic tissue, known as radiomics (radiomics), that are not readily visible on conventional computed tomography (CT) scans.

REDMOD also automatically identifies and outlines the pancreas, separating it from nearby organs and tissues. This process eliminates the need for specialists to manually trace the organ's boundaries, reducing the inconsistencies that can arise when different people perform the task.

AI Finds Hidden Cancer Signals Years Before Diagnosis

To evaluate the system, the researchers examined abdominal CT scans from 219 patients treated at multiple hospitals. At the time of their scans, experienced radiologists had found no evidence of pancreatic cancer. However, every patient in this group was subsequently diagnosed with the disease.

The scans had been taken at different intervals before diagnosis. For 87 patients (40%), the images were obtained 3 to 12 months earlier. Another 76 patients (35%) had been scanned 12 to 24 months before diagnosis, while 56 (25%) had undergone imaging more than 24 months earlier (up to around 3 years). In nearly two thirds (64%) of the patients, the cancer developed in the head of the pancreas.

The researchers compared these images with CT scans from 1243 people who remained free of pancreatic cancer for up to three years afterward. The comparison group was matched according to age, sex, and the dates of their scans.

Patients who eventually developed pancreatic cancer had an average age of 69, with ages ranging from 34 to 88. Those in the comparison group were 64 years old on average, with the same age range of 34 to 88.

REDMOD successfully identified subtle imaging signatures associated with pancreatic cancer an average of 475 days before patients received their clinical diagnoses. These early warning signs had previously gone undetected during routine radiological assessments.

"This temporal window holds profound significance, as attaining such early detection would substantially augment the probability of cure and improved survival," highlight the researchers.

"In fact, modelling studies indicate that increasing the proportion of localized [pancreatic ductal carcinomas] from 10% to 50% would more than double survival rates, thereby underscoring that the timing of diagnosis is the single most critical determinant of survival outcomes," they add.

The results also showed that REDMOD was substantially better than experienced radiologists at recognizing early cancer signals.

The AI achieved a sensitivity of 73%, compared with 39% for radiologists. Sensitivity measures how effectively a diagnostic method identifies people who actually have the disease, rather than overlooking genuine cases.

The difference was even more pronounced when researchers examined scans taken more than two years before the patients were diagnosed. In these cases, REDMOD achieved a detection rate of 68%, nearly three times the 23% recorded by radiologists.

The researchers also assessed how well the system could recognize scans from people without pancreatic cancer. In an independent group of 539 patients from several hospitals, REDMOD correctly classified just over 81% of scans as cancer free. It performed even better on the publicly available US National Institutes of Health NIH-PCT dataset (80 patients), correctly identifying 87.5% as free of pancreatic cancer.

Additional testing suggested that the early warning signs detected by REDMOD were consistent over time. When the researchers analyzed scans taken from the same patients several months apart, the system produced matching results in 90 to 92% of cases. This consistency strengthened the evidence that the AI was identifying meaningful changes associated with the disease.

Could AI Transform Early Pancreatic Cancer Detection?

Despite the promising findings, the researchers caution that several questions remain unanswered. One limitation is that the study population did not include a sufficiently diverse range of ethnic backgrounds, which could affect how well the technology performs across different populations.

The system must also undergo prospective testing, particularly among people at increased risk of pancreatic cancer, before researchers can determine whether it will be effective in everyday clinical practice.

Even with these limitations, the findings suggest that AI could eventually help doctors identify pancreatic cancer while it is still at a much more treatable stage, potentially improving survival for patients who would otherwise receive a late diagnosis.

The researchers conclude: "This study validates REDMOD as a fully automated AI framework capable of identifying the imaging signatures of stage 0 [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] in normal pancreas, achieving this with substantial lead times and performance superior to expert radiologists."

They add: "While prospective validation is paramount to confirm clinical utility, the REDMOD framework represents a significant advance towards shifting the paradigm for sporadic [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] from a late-stage symptomatic diagnosis to proactive pre-clinical interception, offering tangible hope for improving outcomes in this challenging disease."
