#5601. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5600. Marvell to acquire optical component maker Lumentum in massive $115B deal

Marvell Technology Inc. today announced plans to acquire Lumentum Holdings Inc. for $115 billion, in one of the largest deals in tech history.

Lumentum investors are set to receive 4.5 Marvell shares for every unit of stock they own. That translates to about $1,132 per share, which is 23.9% higher than the company’s last unaffected stock price.

Investors, however, weren’t so sanguine about the deal. Marvell’s shares fell almost 13%, while Lumentum’s fell almost 19%. Chalk it up, again, to recent investor worry that the promised growth from artificial intelligence infrastructure may not last forever.

Marvell provides networking equipment for data centers and telecommunications infrastructure. Many of its products use fiber-optic cables to transmit data. Lumentum, in turn, makes components for fiber-optic network devices such as those offered by Marvell. The acquisition will give the latter company more control over its supply chain, which could enable it to more closely align upstream components’ design with its requirements.

Optical networks use laser emitters to generate the light which they transmit data. Lumentum sells a line of lasers based on indium phosphide, a semiconducting material that generates light more efficiently than silicon. The product family includes modular and continuous wave devices. Modulated lasers are used to physically connect servers to the host data center’s optical network, while continuous wave lasers power longer-range network links.

Lumentum also makes single-mode optical amplifiers. Such devices strengthen the laser signals that travel through long-haul carrier networks to reduce data transmission errors.

Last year, the company debuted a laser optimized for co-packaged optics, or CPO, chips. Such chips enable servers to connect to the host data center’s network without expensive modules called transceivers that are usually needed for the task. CPO technology has emerged as an important focus of Marvell’s growth strategy. Its chip design business can help customers integrate CPO modules into their custom artificial intelligence accelerators.

Lumentum doesn’t focus solely on the laser component market. It uses a material called indium gallium arsenide to make analog photodetectors, which customers can use to monitor their optical networks for errors. The company also sells optical circuit switches. Such devices use tiny mirrors to coordinate the flow of traffic, which removes the need to turn data into electrical signals and thereby saves power.

Notably, Lumentum will also give Marvell a presence in the industrial equipment market. The former company makes high-power lasers for cutting and welding machines. It’s unclear what will happen to that part of Lumentum’s product portfolio following the deal. After a large acquisition, companies sometimes spin off newly absorbed business units that don’t align with their core focus.

“By bringing together two leaders with highly complementary technologies, exceptional talent and specialized manufacturing capabilities, we intend to help shape the next era of AI connectivity and create exceptional stockholder value,” said Marvell Chief Executive Officer Matt Murphy.

The chipmaker expects to close the acquisition in the first half of 2028. The combined company will be led by Murphy, while Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston will join the board along with two of the optical component supplier’s directors.

Marvell expects the deal to become accretive to its adjusted earnings per share within a year of closing. In the longer term, the company hopes to achieve annual run-rate cost savings of more than $1 billion and accelerate revenue growth. Marvell estimates that Lumentum will expand its total addressable market to $550 billion.

#5598. Tennessee Voters Opt To Ban State-Level Property Taxes

Voters in Tennessee are projected to approve Amendment 2, which bans any future statewide property tax and enshrines the prohibition in the state constitution.

Tennessee has not had a statewide property tax since 1949, though the state Legislature technically retained the constitutional authority to create one. Instead, property taxes are levied at the local level.

At 11 p.m. ET on Tuesday, the measure had 66.4% support with 82% of votes reporting, according to The Associated Press. An amendment to the Tennessee Constitution passes if it gets at least 50% support, and the number of “yes” votes is more than half of all votes cast for governor.

"It ensures that the state cannot impose property taxes again, putting taxpayers’ interests first and reinforcing local control," said Republican state Rep. Tandy Darby, who sponsored the amendment.

Amendment 2 would not prevent counties and municipal authorities from levying property taxes, but would prohibit the General Assembly from issuing property taxes now and in the future.

In order to change that, the state constitution would have to be amended once more, which would require a two-thirds vote in two legislative sessions and voter approval.

Republican Gov. Bill Lee came out in support of the initiative. It's supported by the National Federation of Independent Business as well as the Tennessee Realtors®.

Conservative nonprofit Tennessee Stands said the amendment "reinforces the principle that private property rights should never be subject to excessive government taxation or the threat of confiscation."

Some Democrats have opposed it on the grounds that the ban does not need to be written into the constitution and should remain a state statute.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. #5597. Palantir beats Q3 forecasts as US commercial revenue overtakes government for first time

Shares of Palantir Technologies Inc. rose more than 1% in late trading today after the big-data analytics company beat third-quarter expectations and raised its full-year revenue guidance for the third time this year.

For the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, Palantir reported adjusted earnings per share of 44 cents, up from 21 cents in the same quarter of last year, on revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 41 cents per share on revenue of $2.18 billion. It was the first quarter in which Palantir’s revenue topped $2 billion.

U.S. commercial revenue overtook U.S. government revenue for the first time in Palantir’s history. Sales to commercial customers in the U.S. reached $984 million, up 148% from a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Government sales rose 96%, to $953 million. Together they took total U.S. revenue to $1.937 billion, up 119% year-over-year.

Palantir closed 212 deals worth at least $1 million in the quarter, including 64 worth $10 million or more. Total contract value rose 6% from a year earlier, to $2.918 billion, after growing 151% in the same period of 2025. U.S. commercial remaining deal value climbed 79%, to $6.517 billion.

Net income more than doubled, to $1.128 billion from $476 million a year earlier, giving the company a 49% net margin. On an adjusted basis, operating income came to $1.427 billion at a 62% margin, and adjusted free cash flow was $1.216 billion. Palantir’s “Rule of 40” score hit 158%. The company ended September holding $10.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents and U.S. Treasury securities.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Alex Karp used the earnings release to argue that what he called the “Sovereign AI movement” is creating “the most dramatic dichotomy between haves and have nots” he has seen in 30 years in business. Governments and companies alike are being forced into one group or the other, “voluntarily or not,” according to Karp. That shift, he said, is “purpose-built for Palantir.”

Looking to the fourth quarter, Palantir expects revenue of $2.649 billion to $2.653 billion and adjusted operating income of $1.640 billion to $1.644 billion. Analysts had forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $2.46 billion.

Full-year revenue guidance now stands at $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion, up from the $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion Palantir forecast in August. U.S. commercial revenue is expected to exceed $3.559 billion, growth of at least 143%, and the company lifted its adjusted operating income outlook to a range of $5.245 billion to $5.249 billion. Adjusted free cash flow for 2026 is now forecast at $4.8 billion to $5 billion.

#5596. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5595. Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem

For buyers, especially first-time buyers, today’s housing affordability crisis (driven by a host of market challenges, from rising mortgage rates to low inventory and lingering inflation) creates many barriers to entry for homeownership. Is there anything agents can actually do at the local level to move the needle and help their clients achieve their homeownership goals?

Four brokerage leaders recently gathered at RISMedia 38th Annual CEO & Leadership Exchange on a panel titled, “Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem,” to say yes and share their tactics and long-term solutions for buyers facing today’s housing affordability problem.

The session, moderated by RISMedia Founder and CEO John Featherston, included panelists Keith Smith, co-owner, Yes Realty Partners, a Keller Williams Alliance Partner; Ennis Antoine, owner and CEO, EA Realty of Georgia; Katey McGrath, vice president, director of operations, Elfant Wissahickon Realtors®; and Ken Baris, CEO, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Jordan Baris Realty.

Here’s a glimpse into some of the questions and answers that provided attendees with some detailed takeaways to help their clients overcome the affordability challenge.

John Featherston: To set the stage, tell us why brokers should care about the housing affordability issue?

Keith Smith: I’m just going to kind of say the awkward thing to the room. Every single one of us makes a living either directly or indirectly from helping people buy and sell. And if we can’t help people buy and sell, we’re not going to be able to put our key in the door. We’re not going to be able to begin our business. Right now, first-time homebuyers can’t buy, and they’re 40? You have Boomers who will not be able to move on. So if we can’t help people do that, this isn’t just a certain entry point. It’s all the way across the board. I think maybe a little bit later we’ll talk about some possible solutions.

Katey McGrath: Obviously it’s good business. And what’s interesting too is at least in our market, the competition for that business is a lot less intense because it is a little bit more work and it’s not as dollar-productive. It’s absolutely more rewarding and more valuable to your communities, but not everybody gets up and says, “I want to sell lower-priced houses.” And so I love new agents getting into the business and focusing on affordability. We love training them up to pre-qualify renters because most of the time the renters don’t know they can buy a house. So it’s a great way to start your real estate business.

And in our company, we have a lot of things that sort of reinforce that culture of homeownership as the most impactful thing you can do in a community. We also create programs in-house that help leverage gift funds to just get people across the line, which I’ll talk about more, but we thread it through the entire “gestalt” of our organization.

John Featherston: What are some of the ground-level tactics that you’re using in your organization?

Katey McGrath: One of the things we do is we train up. If you get a call for a rental, find out if they are capable of qualifying for homeownership. We lean on our lenders. I rely on them and have a high level of expectation that they’re going to understand the down payment programs and the grant programs and the ability to stack them. We have a program called Building Equity where we crowdfund it. The partners of the company seeded it and now every agent in my company gives $5 to $50 every time they sell a house. We have a nice little fund, and we make a gift to anyone who buys a house for $250,000 or less in the city of Philadelphia. The only question we ask is, are you going to move into it?

We find that we can leverage that. If our lenders want to participate in the program and be on our website, they have to match that gift. We just want to keep the level of homeownership in Philadelphia as high as possible. And we also want people to consider other neighborhoods, other house sizes and conditions that maybe the people saving up for their dream homes are not looking at.

John Featherston: Ennis, how do you educate agents to help them find homes their buyers afford?

Ennis Antoine: When talking to my agents, I have to remind them first, you have to learn to stack resources. And what that means is, get involved in the city, the county and third-party companies like Georgia Dreams and ask them, “What programs do you have available to assist with down payment assistance?” In Atlanta, we have a program where the mayor wants to have 20,000 affordable homes built by 2030, so he has instructed his people to have this agency set aside funds to help buyers with down payment assistance; you have to live in our community for five years and it’s forgivable where you don’t have to pay back those funds. The goal is educating your agents on what funds are available and then once they’re educated, educate the buyers on what to expect and to set realistic expectations.

John Featherston: Are you seeing or anticipating any improvement in affordability issues from the ROAD to Housing Act?

Ennis Antoine: I chaired the FPC advisory committee (Federal Political Coordinators under NAR), and we worked on that bill for two years and got it passed. Now here’s the key, though. It is only an incentive. It’s going to take each one of us to inform our city councilmen and mayors on what’s available, and to pass these bills to say, “Hey, listen, how can we incentivize people to buy a home?” And then second, when it comes to housing supply, that’s going to take a while because we have an inventory shortage. It’s not going to happen overnight, but we have to be patient because it’s only a framework on what could happen if we partner with our city council and Realtor® organizations.

John Featherston: Ken, why is it critical to approach the affordability issue as far as you can see? And is it relevant to the specific markets that you’re now serving?

Ken Baris: Affordability is relative. Somebody who says “I can’t afford” is maybe a kid who grew up in a town, can’t afford to be in the town now, but they may be able to afford in another community. It’s being able to understand the benefits people can get. So for instance, Bank of America’s community reinvestment program with a grant of $17,500. We have a mortgage partnership, and we make sure anyone who will qualify for that is going to get that grant and use Bank of America because it’s good sense for the clients.

And if you are really astute about the business, you have people who are tenants—they don’t know they can afford to purchase. You can train people to purchase. You can help people improve their credit: Higher credit score, lower interest rate. You can train people to do things like say, “I will fall in like with four properties. I will not fall in love with one.” Because if you fall in like with four and we make four lower offers, we actually can turn you into a buyer and something more affordable by being willing to present offers. So we inspire a team to do the work and take the time and good things happen for clients.

We use foyersavings.com. A very interesting website; it has three things. Number one, it gives you an ability to save money at an okay interest rate or a good interest rate so that your money builds. Number two, it gives a modest down payment assistance with $600 credit of the first $10,000 you have, you get 6% additional in interest back. That’s not huge, but it’s something.

And three, it shows programs from all over—banks, lenders, community program—that provide grants. You may not know all the programs in your own market that are available. Foyer goes after these programs and makes them available to people that use the site. So it’s just being aware of these things, using your method of communication to get the information out, inspiring people to understand what they can do. If you don’t buy somewhere, you’re going to make somebody else wealthier.

John Featherston: A follow up to that, because you’re going into a lot of the nuances that help new buyers enter the marketplace. Have you made a concerted effort within your firm to make this type of training and education a competitive differentiator in your organization?

Ken Baris: Hugely. I find units to be sexy, not just high prices. And if you have salespeople that are in more affordable communities and they’re trained for these programs, they do better. Another thing that we’ll do is we’ll send out emails of successful buyers. “John thought he was going to rent. We let him know that we thought he could purchase, and the good news for John is we were right. You might be in the same position. Let’s get together.” And that’s the kind of communication we’re doing. I can’t change somebody’s income, but I could help them learn how to save more, how to improve their credit and how to get down payment assistance. $17,500 can make somebody from not a buyer to a buyer. And it’s a gift. It’s not a loan.

John Featherston: How are you and your agents getting past the current rhetoric that we hear among young people when they say they’re never going to be able to buy a home?

Katey McGrath: One of the biggest myths is that you think you need 20% down. And so it’s education, education, education, myth busting, destigmatizing these programs. It’s super important for young people in your community, but also make sure that your agents feel that way. And it’s great because like I said, the younger agents eat it up and it keeps them busy early in their career.

Ennis Antoine: I put pen to paper. So as far as paying $2,000 a month in rent, I’m saying, let’s talk about this for a second. A landlord just received $24,000 from you for one year. You say I’m staying there for three or four years. Then you have nothing to show for it. Whereas if you bought a home or a condominium, you pay this amount each month, you would have a tax write off and within four or five years, you’ll see a 4% or 5% increase in the value of the property. You can sell that property, walk away with cash, get the tax write off on your tax returns. And so if it was me, I would buy and invest and start to build wealth.

And if you build wealth, you can get a larger home and pay less money. So the key here is you’re a smart person. Let’s make a smart decision. Let’s buy.

Keith Smith: I want to pivot a little bit. We’re talking about how we can make a difference. Just last year through a land trust we put together 40 permanent affordable new construction units. I’m in Charlottesville with the second-highest cost of living in the state of Virginia, the second-highest cost of housing in Virginia. But we were able to do 40 of them. And the way we did this is what I call the four pillars: The local government, the private sector folks—developers, builders, real estate agents, the nonprofits and the people all of us serve. You got to get them into a room. You’ve got to get them all to go into the conversation. We put buyers and sellers together. We negotiate deals together. We put people together that maybe do not want to talk to one another, but they talk to people that get to the end result. And how you put those four pillars together is you show up to the meetings and you do what we all do every day very well, which is negotiate and put people together.

John Featherston: Why isn’t the real estate community playing a more pivotal role than every one of the communities, perhaps the most critical role as far as supporting homeownership?

Katey McGrath: I think everybody in this room is a connector. It’s what we love about what we do. And I think that our credibility and our expertise can help save money in these instances. The earlier we get involved in these conversations, the less mistakes the people with good intentions are going to make to make things more expensive. But also, the credibility that we have as a community member, right? So people are coming to us to buy houses, people are coming to us for education, people are coming to us to build generational wealth for their family. And then we can go to city council, we can go to the state reps, we can go to the zoning meetings and add all of that to just sort of be both sides of the issue.

Housing is bipartisan, so if you can get people together, you have that credibility, everything just becomes more productive and less expensive.

John Featherston: Getting people together over the issue of housing is a common denominator all of us can agree on. When Ennis said, local teachers, first responders, police, essential services, can’t afford to live in the community they’re serving, that is not a unique problem. That’s a problem that permeates around the nation. So the solutions have to be done locally.

Ennis Antoine: That’s correct. So I remind everyone, it doesn’t matter what company you work for, there is a percentage in every company where you deal with first-time homebuyers. It doesn’t have to be your main part of your business, but it should be a part of your business because to whom much is given, much is required. And we must always lead by example because the goal here is homeownership. What can we do? It’s all an education process. In every office, there are agents who are very passionate about their community. Support them, enhance them, show up when they need some help.

They will find a surgeon to have vibrant communities. We need a mixture of people in the community who are willing to work together, live together because we call it a village. And as real estate professionals, we are the fiber of the community. We are the voice of real estate and private property rights do matter.

Ken Baris: Something interesting we did some years ago, we listed 300 brand new two-family homes in Newark, New Jersey. And they were beautiful. The challenge was getting people in. So we had the builder prearrange financing, and we had them buy down the rate. And so it was a much lower interest rate, which lowered the payments. And then we also had the builder give a brand-new computer to every purchaser for one of the units because many of them were going to have kids and they would not have money left over for a new computer. And we thought that was very important. And then when certain buyers were tight, we then created a program where they were giving 5% toward closing costs, and if you get people to pay money toward closing costs, you also make it more affordable.

Keith Smith: “Connected” was the right word. I’ve been in this space for 15 years, and I would hear from elected officials, “Well, I don’t understand what the developer is saying.” The developer’s saying, “I don’t understand what the elected official is saying.” And then the nonprofits don’t understand anybody, and the poor folks that we’re trying to serve are left out there in the dark. Being a connector, that is the perfect word. That’s what we do. We connect and are able to put those four pillars together and put a developer and an elected official who really wants to do the right thing, together. The seller doesn’t trust the buyer; the buyer doesn’t trust the seller. We connect and we put people together and just get that conversation rolling. That’s how you do 40 new construction units in the second-highest cost-of-living area in the state of Virginia and everybody walks away smiling. I didn’t do anything really genius. I just put people in the room and said, start talking.

John Featherston: If you could do one thing to help move this affordability issue forward, what would you do?

Ennis Antoine: The one thing I would do is educate my colleagues and challenge them to get involved. It’s easy to write a check, but it’s amazing what happens when you show up. As a leader, when we show up, our people will follow. So as leaders, show up.

Ken Baris: I think just doing a better job of educating consumers because there’s a lot of buyers that don’t know their buyers. Not everyone will be able to afford. They’ve never always been able to, but there’s many more out there.

Katey McGrath: I’m going to go a little more philosophical. Just remember how important homeownership is to every metric in the community. It reduces crime. It increases education rates. It can lower the temperature in a zip code. It extends life expectancy, but most importantly, it builds generational wealth and creates health outcomes in that community that lift everybody up. And if you internalize that, you’re going to be happier when you go to work. You’re going to have more patience to deal with the hard clients that you’re not going to make a lot of money on and just feel great at the end of the day.

Keith Smith: Invest the one asset you can’t make more of, which is your time. Show up and over time, you’ll make a difference. And of those affordable housing units, every single key I handed to somebody, they were in tears. They never thought they were going to get into the homeownership game. It’s not about the check. It’s about the tears, and it makes a difference.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5594. 42AI launches with $62.5M to predict how traders act when markets turn volatile

Israeli artificial intelligence startup 42AI launched today with $62.5 million in funding to build what it calls a behavioral world model.

Its first customers are brokerages that want to know how individual traders will act when markets turn volatile. 42AI offers software that estimates the odds of each choice a person might make in a given situation. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch.

The company turns what it knows about a person into mathematical representations of personality traits, and a transformer-based world model works out the probabilities from there. A separate language model writes up which traits and context drove each prediction.

42AI says a brokerage can see what each client is likely to trade over the next 24 hours, including the instrument, the direction and the volume. If clients look set to pile into the same trade, a risk desk can hedge before the exposure lands on its book. Know-your-customer checks done at onboarding are one source of input, and the model also weighs how often a client calls and the sentiment in their voice.

Ten large brokerages are working with 42AI, which charges either a flat fee or a percentage of the value it helps generate. Revenue has reached seven figures, Gal-Or said, without giving a precise number.

By the company’s account, one brokerage gained about $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging. The company also claims 98% accuracy on trades. That figure tracks whether trading flows land inside a predicted range, according to Gal-Or, and does not measure whether every individual trade was predicted correctly.

Three years of research went into the model. Thousands of people took psychological assessments in the first study, and by the time the team moved on to government and biobank datasets, the sample had passed 2 million. Customer data now spans about 30 million people.

Chief Technology Officer Ehud Ezra and three co-authors described one piece of the work in a paper posted in February. Their Large Behavioral Model adapts an 8 billion-parameter version of Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama 3.1 to predict a person’s strategic choices from a detailed psychometric profile.

Asked whether a brokerage could turn those predictions against its own clients, Ezra called it “a valid concern.” The founders pointed to regulation, monitoring and an internal ethics committee as checks on that kind of use.

Gaming, fraud prevention and cybersecurity are the next markets 42AI is exploring, with helping robots and AI agents understand people as a longer-term goal. Wherever it runs, the model loses accuracy when it misses outside influences, such as a trader acting on a colleague’s advice. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said.

The $62.5 million, which 42AI describes as seed funding, came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years. Amir Gal-Or, the startup’s co-founder and chairman, founded Infinity Group. Dan Shechtman, who won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is among the advisers to the research team. 42AI plans to raise more money.

#5593. Democrats Regain House and Senate In Midterms Defined By Affordability Concerns

Democrats rode affordability concerns to major wins Tuesday, retaking control of the House and Senate and flipping multiple districts.

Democrats flipped Senate seats in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, North and South Carolina and picked up a swath of seats in the House to win both chambers of Congress, according to AP projections. They've spent the year hammering Republicans on affordability and housing costs.

The 2026 elections, in which all of the 435 seats in the House and 35 in the Senate were up for election, as well as a swath of real estate and housing related measures. Both Democrats and Republicans have listed priorities to improve housing affordability in coming years.

"Tonight’s Democratic sweep shuffles control of the legislative branch, but the economic impact, which is fundamental for the U.S. housing market, is far less clear," says Realtor.com® Senior Economist Jake Krimmel. "Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen."

Housing issues have been a dominant note in 2026, as Americans struggle with affordability. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hit its highest level in three years last month before dipping back to 7.24% last week, according to Fannie Mae. The national average gas price is $4.14 compared to $3.03 a year ago, according to AAA. President Donald Trump has pledged to focus on affordability issues.

"President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Realtor.com in a statement on Tuesday morning.

Ingle noted that Trump in his second term had signed an executive order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows, and "cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs."

"The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation," he said.

Congress passed a bipartisan housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, this summer. But it will take years for some of those changes to take effect in the market. And lawmakers expect states and local governments must implement some changes.

The Trump administration, meantime, has undertaken other changes such as encouraging more innovation in the homebuilding sector and reducing rules for some housing, like manufactured homes. It's also sought to limit the impact of institutional investors in the housing market.

"I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!," Trump posted to X late Tuesday, as major news outlets projected Democrats would take control of the House after flipping half a dozen seats. Trump later told the New York Times he would accept the results of the election.

The economist Krimmel says that one "wildcard" to keep an eye on is how the election outcome impacts Trump's war with Iran.

"Many Democrats have been vocal critics of the conflict, which has sparked inflationary oil supply shortages," he says. "A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates. However, a lot of uncertainty remains. Wanting the conflict to end, and finding terms that work for all involved are two different things."

Democrats marked the evening with several key wins in both the House and the Senate.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews flipped the Senate seat formerly held by Republican Lindsey Graham. Andrews beat Graham's sister, Darlene Graham, who had been picked by Trump.

And Democrat James Talarico flipped a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat in almost a century to be elected to the Senate.

Democrats had several early victories. Democratic former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper flipped the state's Senate seat, replacing Republican Thom Tillis, who chairs the Senate's Financial Institutions and Consumer Protection Subcommittee. Democrat Jamie Ager also flipped a North Carolina House district.

"We knew that the chaos and corruption in Washington were hurting our people," Cooper said in a speech. "Today, you said 'this has to stop.'"

Pennsylvania saw three formerly Republican seats picked up by Democrats including Janelle Stelson, Paige Cognetti and Bob Brooks. They ousted incumbents Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan Jr. and Scott Perry.

In New Jersey, Tom Kean Jr. lost re-election after an extended absence fueled national headlines. Meantime, in Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown returned to Congress after campaigning heavily against incumbent Jon Husted, attacking him over his prior support of data centers.

"Politics should never ever be about two private clubs who are more interested in beating up each other than they are in solving problems," said Josh Turek, who flipped a Senate seat in Iowa for Democrats.

On Truth Social, Trump posted a photo of a red hat with the word "veto." He has repeatedly criticized Democrats this year saying their policies drive up housing and other costs.

Trump told Fox News late on Tuesday night that he would not shy away from using presidential vetos to block "crazy" measures advanced by Democrats in Congress.

"I have the power of veto, and the power of veto, you know, it's impervious," the president said.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, who won election in Louisiana, defended Republicans' economic actions in remarks before midnight. He said Americans would "suffer" if Democrats use control of Congress to enact "retribution" over the next two years.

"From the first day of this election we knew that to keep the House and sustain the majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson said. "It's very, very difficult to overcome."

But Johnson said an agenda of "common sense" would lead Republicans to take back the House in 2028.

"Republicans have much more work to do," he said. "The new Congress doesn't change that at all."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5592. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5591. Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO

Anthropic PBC today published an updated version of the S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering.

The original document, which the company released last Monday, didn’t contain its third-quarter financial results. The new version reveals that Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue during the three months ended Sept. 30. That’s more than 11 times more than what it made a year earlier, but represents a deacceleration in quarter-over-quarter growth. Anthropic’s top line grew 47% on a quarterly basis, down from 144% three months earlier.

The artificial intelligence provider faces multipronged competition from open-source models, OpenAI Group PBC and tech giants such as Google LLC. The Alphabet Inc.’s newest model, Gemini 4 Carbon, outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks.

Anthropic is investing heavily in training infrastructure to stay ahead of the competition. The company took a $5 billion charge in the third quarter because demand for computing hardware was higher than expected, which required it to purchase hardware at a premium. Hardware bought on short notice is more expensive than Anthropic’s usual capacity commitments, which it books 12 to 18 months before they’re needed.

The AI provider also took a $2 billion charge in connection with its non-cash employee donation matching program. That left Anthropic with a $536 million operating loss at the end of the third quarter. Three months earlier, it posted $974 million in operating income. Anthropic’s adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation and charitable contributions, jumped by $300 million on a quarterly basis to $2.5 billion.

The company had $895.4 billion in outstanding infrastructure commitments as of Sept 30. Leases signed with Google LLC and Broadcom Inc. accounted for nearly a third of that sum. In April, the two companies agreed to supply Anthropic with several gigawatts of computing power powered by the search giant’s TPU chips, which Broadcom helped design. The AI provider also has computing deals with Amazon.com Inc., Oracle Corp. and SpaceX Technologies Corp. that are each worth more than $100 billion.

Anthropic plans to not only rent more computing capacity but also build its own data centers. The company’s purchase commitments jumped from $55 billion at the end of 2025 to about $314 billion in the third quarter.

Alongside the new financial figures, Anthropic’s revised S-1 filing provides an update about its efforts to mitigate AI risks. According to the document, the company is considering “to require human review and approval of certain” research tasks that are currently performed automatically by its models. It believes that its models will soon be capable of “dramatically” accelerating AI development.

Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it plans to raise through its public offering. According to Bloomberg, the company hopes to at least match the $86.2 billion that SpaceX pulled in when it listed its shares earlier this year. Reuters reported that Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

#5590. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5589. Rack-scale AI: How Dell and AMD are building infrastructure

Dell Technologies Inc. and its partner Advanced Micro Devices Inc. face similar competitive pressures. Both tech powerhouses operate in a business climate where success is now measured across central processing units, graphics processing units, rack-scale systems, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar.

The pressure to compete across those measures underscores what theCUBE Research has termed “Engineering Velocity.” Since the Dell Technologies World event in May, AMD and Dell have not slowed their pace of collaborations and announcements.

AMD and Dell are working to build enterprise AI infrastructure that can keep pace with changing workloads and customer requirements.

“In AI infrastructure, the winner may not be the company with the best benchmark on keynote day,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante. “It will more likely be the company whose engineering system learns, validates and improves the entire platform faster than anyone else.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale” and its past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

A cornerstone of the Dell and AMD relationship is the server giant’s PowerEdge portfolio. Dell expanded its PowerEdge server line in May and has followed that up with additional details surrounding the integration of AMD processors.

The two companies have pursued a strategy designed to facilitate server consolidation as agentic AI drives a surge in demand for general-purpose compute. Agents rely heavily on CPUs, yet data centers don’t have a lot of extra room to add servers in rooms already stacked with GPUs.

Systems powered by AMD processors will deliver 70% gen-over-gen performance gains and can fold 13 servers from Dell’s 14th PowerEdge generation into one, according to Pradyumna Narendra, product planner and senior consultant at Dell.

“For every 10 to 13 servers you replace, you get so much of that productivity gain back because now you can do that with one server,” he told theCUBE. “When you expand that across data centers, that’s like an accelerating effect that you get to capitalize from.”

Dell and AMD must also accommodate a wealth of AI use cases and the accompanying demand for compute. Dell’s three-rack-unit server requires less power for cooling than a two-unit equivalent, allowing customers to pack more computing power into each rack, according to Narendra.

“By deploying servers that are slightly larger in package, you deliver more density at a rack level, which seems sometimes counterintuitive,” he explained. “As AI accelerates, inferencing and agentic AI around it will accelerate and grow faster. As these use cases scale out, you get exponential growth in the need for compute.”

Beyond server consolidation, Dell and AMD have been steadily enhancing a modular solution to simplify AI deployment and scaling: the Dell AI Platform with AMD.

The on-premises enterprise AI solution integrates AMD Instinct accelerators and EPYC processors with Dell PowerEdge servers, PowerSwitch networking and PowerScale storage for model training, fine-tuning and high-throughput inference. The platform is designed to let customers begin with configurations that meet current workloads and expand compute and GPU density over time, without rearchitecting.

“What we’re finding is customers want modular solutions. They want to think about [solutions] across the whole platform,” said Varun Chhabra, senior vice president of product marketing and infrastructure solutions group at Dell, in a discussion with theCUBE. “Compute, storage, networking [and] GPU. The software framework on top of it, the models: Have they all been tested? Have they all been validated?”

Dell has integrated the AMD ROCm software stack into the platform to support training, fine-tuning and serving large language models on-premises. The modular platform lets customers begin with smaller deployments and expand on the same infrastructure, according to Chhabra.

“You can start small with these composable units of storage, compute, networking, pre-integrated with AMD Instinct and EPYC CPUs with the ROCm software as well as the open ecosystem that sits on top of it,” he said. “We test it, we validate it, and the customers can use it and once they start seeing value in it, they know they can scale in a modular way with the same frameworks.”

Dell announced support for AMD Instinct MI350P PCI Express GPUs in its PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers beginning in July, giving enterprises another option for scaling agentic and generative AI deployments. It also represents an important boost in memory bandwidth which matters in time-to-first-token latency.

The MI350P offers 144 gigabytes of HBM3E memory, which can be a key differentiator for inference performance, according to Mike Darby, senior manager of business development, Instinct Data Center GPUs, at AMD, during an appearance on theCUBE.

“It’s a lot of memory, but it’s also HBM3E, so [it has] an amazing amount of bandwidth,” he said. “The main use case being inference: It’s all about that latency, time to first token [and] the user experience, so that your attention span doesn’t move somewhere else while you’re waiting for your response.”

AMD and Dell’s collaboration on PCIe integration has another angle worth watching. AMD’s PCIe-based GPU supports air-cooled deployments, providing users with a path to deploy AI within existing data center infrastructure.

As the tech industry has encountered resistance in recent months to the buildout of large data centers across the U.S., concerns have centered on the environmental impact and use of water-based cooling systems. Separately, Dell found that, as it deployed its next-generation PowerEdge servers, some enterprise customers were still not prepared to adopt liquid cooling within data centers.

“Working with Dell, we added a PCI card to our air-coolable roadmap for GPU Instinct so that it fit in more Dell PowerEdge servers that go to the broader enterprise,” said Robert Hormuth, corporate vice president of architecture and strategy for the Data Center Solutions Group at AMD, during a conversation with theCUBE. “Not everybody is adopting direct liquid cooling.”

Dell’s work with AMD this year has extended beyond joint product announcements. In June, the two companies announced a partnership with the University of Cambridge to establish a Sovereign AI Innovation Lab (SAIL) in the United Kingdom.

The collaboration is designed to help advance the next generation of AI infrastructure and AI-powered scientific breakthroughs. It builds on Cambridge’s expanded AI research infrastructure, including the Zenith AI supercomputer, powered by fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators integrated into Dell infrastructure.

Dell and AMD have also collaborated in recent months on a telecom initiative with AT&T Inc. Telecom data is a heavy lift when it comes to AI, with AT&T having processed over one trillion tokens to train models. AMD has provided the high-performance hardware foundation for both training and inference workloads involving the OTel 2.0 models developed through the Open Telco AI initiative.

Dell integrated this technology with AI-optimized servers for telecom environments to create a production-grade foundation for operators across data-intensive, real-world network environments. OTel 2.0’s training infrastructure uses Dell’s PowerEdge XE9785 server configured with eight MI355X GPUs.

The alliance between Dell and AMD highlights a key development in the growing AI infrastructure market: There are plenty of opportunities for competition. Both Dell and AMD appear committed to building portfolios that offer enterprise choices in AI processing solutions.

“AMD didn’t present its new products … as ‘respectable alternatives,’” Vellante said. “It claimed outright leadership across CPUs, GPUs, rack-scale performance, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar. It extended the argument across enterprise AI, robotics, ultra-low-latency inference and a rapidly expanding partner ecosystem.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)
