#5588. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5587. Apple’s stock drops as new CEO John Ternus delivers his first earnings call

Apple Inc. just delivered its first earnings call since new Chief Executive John Ternus took over the company from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, and the results beat expectations on the top and bottom lines. But the company missed expectations on iPhone sales and offered disappointing guidance going forward, and the stock fell in late trading.

The company reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.10 per share, comfortably ahead of Wall Street’s target of $1.99 per share. Revenue for the period rose 12%, to $114.48 billion, easing past the $113.39 billion analyst forecast. All told, its net income came to $30.71 billion at the end of the quarter, up from just $27.46 billion one year earlier.

When Ternus (pictured) stepped up to relieve Cook in the CEO’s chair a couple of months ago, he realized he was stepping into a job with sky-high expectations, following in the footsteps of two of the most successful company leaders in American history. Steve Jobs was credited with revolutionizing consumer devices, while Cook took the company to spectacular new heights thanks to his operational expertise, establishing it as one of the world’s most iconic brands.

The weight of expectations is reflected by Apple’s enormous valuation. According to Oppenheimer analyst Martin Yang, the iPhone maker is trading at about 36 times next year’s expected earnings. That represents a premium compared with the rest of the technology market, even though its earnings are only expected to grow 1% this year, slower than many of its peers.

Nonetheless, investors have piled into Apple because it’s something of an outlier in the artificial intelligence boom. While its rivals are all spending hundreds of billions of dollars on building data centers, Apple has remained extremely capital-efficient, pouring cash into share buybacks and dividends for shareholders. That has given the company a strong margin for safety, but its position could still be threatened if Ternus can’t find a way to speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

The company has already been criticized for its lackluster performance in AI. Its long-awaited Siri AI chatbot finally arrived during the past quarter, but it came across as stale the moment it arrived. By the time it had launched, it had already been surpassed by autonomous AI agents such as Dots and Muse that can perform multistep tasks on behalf of users, while Siri is still fumbling around with answering questions.

Analysts wanted to know if Apple is planning to offer more AI features through subscriptions or services, but Ternus declined to reveal what the company’s future plans are. But he insisted that Apple has “lots of opportunities” for monetization in future. “One example is the hardware side, right?” he said. “It offers a compelling reason for upgrading or switching.”

Jacob Bourne of Emarketer told SiliconANGLE that Apple’s stock premium is likely linked to the growing concerns some investors have over the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom, which is being driven by all of Apple’s big tech peers. “Its tepid approach to AI infrastructure spending has helped to preserve its cash flow, and through strategic partnerships Apple may be able to strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers,” Bourne said. “But Apple faces its own challenges as AI-enabled devices such as smart glasses could eventually challenge the iPhone’s central role in iOS. Apple’s long-term advantage will hinge on combining its hardware strengths with compelling AI capabilities in a way that preserves its reputation.”

In the meantime, the pressure is on for Apple to give consumers more reasons to buy its expensive devices, especially as the costs of those products have been getting higher. Today’s report was the first full quarter of higher-priced Apple products following a price hike in June that stemmed from the rising cost of memory supplies and other components.

The price of most iPhone handsets was hiked by around $100, but consumers didn’t appear to punish Apple. On the contrary, iPhone revenue was a bright spot, reaching $57.58 billion in the quarter, up 17% from a year earlier and above the $56.54 billion consensus estimate. That’s despite the quarter including only eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales and none of the new flagship device, the iPhone Duo.

Apple needed a good quarter from the iPhone because its main growth engine, the services business, is slowing. Revenue there came to $31.57 billion, just below the Street’s forecast of $31.58 billion, growing less than 10% during the quarter, its slowest rate of growth since September 2022. The business includes revenue from a wide range of products and services, such as iCloud storage, AppleCare warranties, App Store fees and licensing revenue from Google LLC for putting its search engine as the default option in the Safari browser.

“We saw strong performance in many service categories, with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising, and a September quarter record in music,” Tetanus told analysts.

Apple saw a better performance in its Mac computer division, with sales of $10.79 billion comfortably topping the Street’s forecast of $9.61 billion. The unit’s revenue grew almost 24% on an annual basis, following the launch of new Mac Studio and Mac Mini laptops in August.

The iPad division was a disaster, however, as sales declined more than 10% from the previous year to $6.3 billion, trailing the Street’s forecast of $6.7 billion. Last month saw the launch of a new iPad Mini model, following the debut of the updated iPad Air back in March, but despite those releases, there has been no flagship model launching this year, and that appears to have hurt the business’ performance. When asked about the miss, Ternus blamed supply constraints and a difficult comparison with last year as the main reasons for its disappointing performance.

Holger Mueller of Constellation Research said today’s earnings call was close to a baptism of fire for Ternus, who had to field analyst’s questions for the first time in his capacity as the company’s new CEO. While Apple’s overall growth was okay, it did not translate those revenue gains to its bottom line. “There is one good explanation that still encourages investors to bet on Apple’s future, namely that there was a substantial increase in R&D spending compared to the previous year, up more than $10 billion in fact,” the analyst said. “The iPhone remains the star of Apple’s portfolio and the company depends on its success more than ever. If iPhone sales don’t grow, that means lower services growth. The introduction of a touchscreen Mac will perhaps finally show if Steve Jobs was right about one thing — that touch on a PC will cannibalize iPad sales.”

The disappointing performance of Apple’s services and iPad units was compounded by what was seen as weak guidance for the current quarter, which includes the peak Christmas sales period. Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh didn’t offer concrete numbers, but said the company expects its revenue to grow by between 7% and 10% in the quarter. Wall Street analysts are looking for higher growth of 11.4%, however. Parekh also revealed that Apple is forecasting its gross margin to fall between 45% and 46%, declining from the fourth quarter.

Apple’s stock fell almost 3% on today’s report, but it’s still up more than 24% in the year to date compared with a gain of just over 10% for the broader S&P 500 index.

#5585. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5584. THE KOREA INDUSTRY DAILY: ROBOTWORLD 2026 to Spotlight Physical AI and AI-Driven Manufacturing With 402 Exhibitors From 17 Countries

Rainbow Robotics, Neuromeka and Samhyun to exhibit Nov. 4â7 near Seoul; NVIDIA and Qualcomm to participate in conference

GOYANG, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ROBOTWORLD 2026 will bring together 402 companies from 17 countries at the Korea International Exhibition Center (KINTEX) Nov. 4â7. The 1,198-booth exhibition will explore how Physical AI and AI-driven manufacturing systems are being developed for industrial applications.

International exhibitors will include Taiwan's Advantech, Japan's FANUC and China's Booster Robotics, PAXINI and Unitree. A Canadian delegation of 10 technology companies will participate in the exhibition and conference, while companies from India and Bangladesh will exhibit at ROBOTWORLD for the first time.

The International Robot Business Conference 2026 will extend the discussion of industrial applications through 36 sessions on Nov. 4â5. Its three tracks â Manufacturing AX (AI transformation), Humanoid with Physical AI and Mobility â will address AI adoption in production, robot intelligence and mobility across industrial and service environments. The Manufacturing AX track will feature presentations by representatives from Qualcomm and Advantech, while a speaker from NVIDIA will present in the Humanoid with Physical AI track. Qualcomm will also sponsor the exhibition.

According to the International Federation of Robotics' World Robotics 2026 report, global industrial robot installations reached a record 603,307 units in 2025, marking an 11% increase from the previous year and surpassing 600,000 units for the first time. Asia accounted for 76% of all newly installed industrial robots, with 457,315 units installed, up 14% year-on-year. Global installations are forecast to reach 655,000 units in 2026, reflecting the continued expansion of industrial automation.

Against this industrial backdrop, the exhibition will explore Physical AI technologies that enable robots to perceive their surroundings, assess conditions and perform physical tasks. Korean exhibitors will address both task intelligence and the platforms and components that enable movement and manipulation.

Rainbow Robotics will exhibit its RBY mobile humanoid and RBQ quadruped series, while Neuromeka will present its Physical Skill Foundation (PSF) technology alongside the EIR humanoid and NAMI mobile humanoid platforms. Neuromeka describes PSF as supporting task execution involving unfamiliar objects and changing work environments. Samhyun will showcase its AXLON actuator series for robot joint actuation, torque control and linear motion, together with the BOLDUM autonomous transport robot for industrial material handling with payloads of up to 3 metric tons.

Beyond individual robots, the exhibition will examine AI-driven manufacturing through systems that combine collaborative robots, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), machine vision and manufacturing software. Exhibitors will demonstrate how process data and material flows can inform robot and equipment operations across production processes.

Humanoid, food-tech and healthcare pavilions will provide focused views of these technologies and their applications. The newly established humanoid pavilion will cover complete robots, actuators, reducers, sensors, controllers and AI software. The food-tech pavilion will feature cooking, serving and kitchen automation. The returning healthcare pavilion will cover surgical, rehabilitation, wearable and care robots, as well as hospital logistics.

Business programs will connect the technology presentations with opportunities for procurement, exports and investment. Export and procurement matchmaking sessions will run Nov. 4â6, with suppliers and prospective buyers matched in advance for one-to-one meetings. A seminar on entering international markets will be held on Nov.5 providing practical information on certification requirements in different countries.

Global Scale-up Day on Nov. 6 will be open to small and medium-sized enterprises as well as startups in AI and robotics seeking investment and growth capital. Conducted entirely in English, the program will bring together venture capital firms, accelerators, strategic investors and M&A specialists.

"With increased participation by global companies and the addition of national and special pavilions, we hope this year's exhibition will showcase the capabilities of Korean robotics companies and expand opportunities for practical cooperation between Korean and international businesses," a ROBOTWORLD representative said.

ROBOTWORLD 2026 will take place at KINTEX Exhibition Center 1, Halls 3â5, in Goyang. Information on exhibitors, conference sessions and business programs are available at https://eng.robotworld.or.kr/.

ROBOTWORLD is an international robotics exhibition covering industrial and service robots, core components, AI software and manufacturing automation solutions, alongside a conference and business programs. ROBOTWORLD 2026 is hosted by South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources (MOTIR) and jointly organized by the Korea Association of AI Robot Industry (KAR), the Korea Institute for Robot Industry Advancement (KIRIA) and the Institute of Control, Robotics and Systems (ICROS).

#5583. Robotics startup Tutor Intelligence nabs $75M investment

Warehouse automation provider Tutor Intelligence Inc. today announced that it has raised $75 million in funding.

Andreessen Horowitz led the Series A investment. It was joined by Union Square Ventures and Neo, which led Tutor’s previous two rounds.

The merchandise that a warehouse processes often arrives on pallets, flat wood structures capable of holding up to several tons. Tutor sells a mobile robotic arm called Cassie that can take packages off a pallet and place them in containers. It’s also capable of performing the opposite operation.

Cassie can process up to 18 items per minute depending on the package type. Its robotic arm is equipped with a vacuum gripper designed to pick up more than 50 pounds. The arm is mounted on a four-wheeled platform that enables Cassie to autonomously travel between different sections of a warehouse.

Automating pallet processing is challenging because the merchandise that a warehouse receives changes over time. Historically, adapting a robotic arm’s workflow to a new item involved manual coding. Cassie uses built-in artificial intelligence models to learn how to pick up new package types automatically.

Tutor also ships its AI models with a second wheeled robot called Sonny. It uses a pair of robotic arms to take items off warehouse shelves and place them in packages. The robot finds the needed items using an array of time-of-flight and stereo cameras. Both camera varieties collect depth data, which makes it easier to determine the distance of an object.

Tutor plans to apply Sonny to additional use cases in the future. In particular, it sees industrial companies using the system to assemble products and perform equipment maintenance. Tutor teaches Sonny’s AI models new tasks in a facility that hosts more than 100 robots. Human experts demonstrate how to perform a task using a remotely controlled robot and the AI models learn by imitation.

“Sonny’s manufacturability at scale makes it an ideal robot not just for most handwork in manufacturing and logistics, but for arbitrary business-critical applications across the physical economy,” Tutor co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Josh Gruenstein wrote in a blog post. “Data collected by our Sonny fleet trains our largest and most capable robot foundation models at the frontier of rate and reliability.”

Tutor sells its robots under a usage-based pricing model. It removes the need for customers to make a large upfront purchase, which lowers the entry barrier. The company disclosed today that the number of facilities where its robots are used has nearly quadrupled over the past year.

Tutor will use its newly raised funding to enhance its AI models and speed up robot production.

#5582. Binance Withdrawals Top FTX Levels in November, but Crypto Liquidity Defies Panic

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Binance withdrawals surged into the billions after a record-breaking $6.3 billion hack, bringing back memories of FTX’s November 2022 collapse. Yet the world’s largest crypto exchange is showing a resilience that could barricade the industry from its darkest chapter.

Binance processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits during the first nine and a half hours after reopening services on November 1, resulting in $3.64 billion in net outflows. According to its October 28 Proof of Reserves data, the exchange held $171 billion in total assets, so the withdrawal wave accounted for just 2.1% of its reported holdings.

Binance withdrawals are BACK!BTC, ETH, BNB, XRP, DOGE, USDT, USDC and more are being re-enabled across supported networks.Binance also says 95% of the stolen assets have already been replaced.Bears were screaming FTX 2.0, desperately hoping for another collapse.

This puts the outflows in perspective: despite the initial rush following the $6.3 billion hack, Binance retained assets worth 47 times the net amount withdrawn. The exchange said withdrawals had begun stabilizing, while deposits remained substantial.

The figures initially look alarming, especially against the backdrop of FTX. The failed exchange suffered $6 billion in net withdrawals over 72 hours before suspending customer withdrawals in November 2022.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

“98% choose to stay. Trust isn’t earned by what you say in good times. It’s earned by what you do in hard times.” – Changpeng Zhao, Binance Founder

Binance has previously said that it had set aside more than $6.34 billion to cover the incident, including $5 billion in the affected token assets. It also reported that partners had frozen approximately $3 billion linked to the attack.

So how does this compare to FTX? This current crisis is fundamentally different from FTX’s collapse. FTX’s withdrawal run exposed a liquidity shortfall tied to customer funds and its relationship with Alameda Research. Binance, by contrast, says it will cover the stolen assets rather than pass the losses to users.

Bitcoin’s reaction offers one of the clearest signs of crypto’s resilience compared with the FTX collapse. Following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, BTC briefly slipped toward $76,700 but held above the closely watched $75,000 support level before recovering toward $79,000. The contrast with November 2022 is stark. Bitcoin fell nearly 10% on November 8 as FTX’s withdrawal crisis intensified, then plunged another 14.4% on November 9 to close near $15,877, after briefly hitting $15,632.

While Binance’s hack triggered billions in withdrawals and market-wide liquidations, Bitcoin has so far avoided the cascading selloff that followed FTX’s implosion. Its ability to defend $75,000 suggests investors are treating the incident as a major exchange security failure rather than evidence of a systemic liquidity crisis across crypto.

Binance has already faced a major financial and regulatory reckoning. In November 2023, the exchange agreed to pay more than $4 billion to resolve U.S. investigations into anti-money laundering and sanctions violations. Founder Changpeng Zhao also pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. He resigned as CEO and paid a separate $50 million fine.

Despite that enormous settlement, Binance continued operating as the world’s largest crypto exchange. The latest hack now presents another test of its financial strength, operational resilience, and ability to maintain customer confidence.

Crypto markets have still felt the shock. Bitcoin and Ethereum fell following the breach, while spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded huge outflows and leveraged positions faced heavy liquidations. However, both major cryptocurrencies partly recovered after hitting lows.

Now, can Binance withdrawals continue to ease? The exchange publishes updated Proof of Reserves data and completes its security review. The comparison with FTX shows the scale of investor concern, but not necessarily the same outcome. Binance has absorbed a major hack, committed to covering customer losses, and resumed withdrawals after billions left the platform.

November has brought back memories of 2022. Binance’s response shows crypto’s largest exchange is determined to keep this crisis from becoming another industry-wide collapse.

#5581. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5579. How Xatoms is using AI to solve the global water crisis

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Every September, Climate Week and Global Citizen Week in New York bring together policymakers, investors and innovators focused on the world’s most pressing problems.

It’s also when Cisco Systems Inc. and Global Citizen recognize the winner of the Global Citizen Prize: Cisco Youth Leadership Award. Cisco and Global Citizen created the award in 2018 to honor a young leader who uses technology to help end extreme poverty, and this year’s recipient may have the most compelling story yet.

Diana Virgovicova (pictured) is the founder and CEO of Xatoms (pronounced “X-Atoms”), a Toronto-based company that uses artificial intelligence and quantum chemistry to design sunlight-activated materials that break down pollutants in water. The award comes with a $250,000 grant, and Xatoms was chosen from more than 2,000 applications.

Most of the AI conversation at Climate Week focused on what AI takes from the planet: power, land and, increasingly, water. Xatoms offers a positive counterpoint, a case study in AI giving back.

Most founders find a market. Virgovicova found a problem the hard way. She grew up in a village of about 800 people in Slovakia, surrounded by farms that used heavy amounts of pesticides. “I got sick when I was 14 years old,” she told me. “I was diagnosed with ovarian cancer because of the water I drank.”

After her diagnosis, she persuaded her mother to go backpacking across Asia. On trains in India, she heard from women facing the same thing. “I learned that there is a girl in Slovakia who got sick. There is a girl in India who’s getting infections. There is a girl in Africa who has to spend long hours every single day searching for clean water,” she said. “So, we need to find a solution, and it is affecting mainly women across the globe.”

Globally, women and girls spend 250 million hours a day collecting water, more than three times the time men and boys spend. “While boys go to school, the girls are responsible for bringing a bucket of water home, and they start missing school very early on,” Virgovicova explained. “It’s an educational, economic and health problem.”

And it’s growing. “We have 2 billion people that don’t have access to clean drinking water, and this number is actually growing because of flooding, climate change,” she said.

One of the more interesting aspects of Xatoms is where it chose to play. Many water treatment efforts target bacteria such as E. coli because the effects are immediate. Xatoms goes after the harder problem: complex industrial pollutants such as pesticides, pharmaceuticals, forever chemicals and heavy metals.

“I think we are forgetting about these complex contaminants because they don’t make us sick tomorrow. They make us sick in 10 years,” she said. “They give us chronic diseases. They cause infertility.” She made a point I hadn’t considered: Scientific progress is making it worse.

“We are able to create better antibiotics, but these better antibiotics are more complex, thus more difficult to destroy in water,” she said. That’s a second-order problem traditional treatment wasn’t built for, and exactly where advanced computational design has an edge.

At 17, while working with a university professor in Slovakia, Virgovicova used quantum chemistry software to design a new molecule that harnesses sunlight to break down water pollutants. That work earned her a Diploma of Excellence from the Swedish Royal Family and a full scholarship to the University of Toronto.

“What is so exciting about this science is that we can use computers to design new materials, and we don’t have to create them in the lab,” she said. “We can see these materials, how they react, and what their properties are before we even synthesize them.”

Quantum chemistry gets far fewer headlines than quantum computing, so I asked her to explain it. “Quantum helps us understand these molecules at a fundamental level, including how the atoms within the molecule interact,” she said. “When we know these fundamental properties, we can understand what makes each molecule good at something, and that helps us design an even better molecule, a better material.”

The output is a photocatalyst powder. “Initially, it was a molecule in a computer, but we were able to synthesize it in a lab,” Virgovicova said. “We put this photocatalytic powder into water. It splits water into OH radicals, and the OH radicals then destroy contaminants.”

Because it’s a catalyst, it isn’t consumed, so a small amount can treat “hundreds of gallons,” she said. Earlier photocatalysts required ultraviolet light; her design works with visible light, such as sunlight or LEDs, eliminating the need for expensive UV reactors.

AI is the accelerant. “It would take a decade if we did it without AI,” she said. “We can do it in 30 days.” That’s the real story for business leaders. Materials discovery has historically been slow, expensive and lab-bound, and Xatoms has transformed it into a computational pipeline.

Here’s where it matters for technology buyers. Data centers consume enormous volumes of water for cooling, and the AI buildout is making that worse. I asked Virgovicova whether Xatoms can flip the script. “There are a lot of problems with contaminants within the data center,” she said. “The data center water needs to be completely clean for cooling,” she said. “We are able to use this catalyst to help reuse the water in data centers.”

This is an underappreciated opportunity. Hyperscalers and neoclouds face mounting pressure over water use, and the industry’s response has largely focused on cooling design. Reuse through improved treatment is a different and more planet-friendly solution.

Xatoms works with Indigenous communities in Canada under longstanding boil-water advisories, as well as in Kenya and South Africa. Virgovicova told me the footprint now includes Japan and Azerbaijan. Every engagement is customized.

“We collect a water sample. Recently, we shipped the sample from Azerbaijan all the way to Canada,” she said. “We identify the contaminant and then determine which of these 88 options would be the best.”

Customers define the outcome. “Some of them want to take yellow water and decolorize it. Some of them have a specific contaminant in mind that they want to remove or reduce,” she said.

Next up are Turkey, where co-founder Kerem Topal Ismail Oglou grew up, and the broader Middle East, driven by textile manufacturing and oil and gas. She also met South Africa’s water minister during Climate Week ahead of a trip to Cape Town.

Being named a global winner of the World Economic Forum’s Water Resilience Challenge opened doors with large enterprises. “We had the chance to interact with some of the biggest Fortune 500 companies, which helped us create pilots and partnerships,” she said.

The Cisco grant is moving directly into execution. “We have more than six major projects coming up, so we need help with lab work,” she said. “We need to figure out the best way to manufacture more materials.” The goal is to “commercialize this technology as fast as we can.”

When I joked that billionaires are hunting for water on Mars while we haven’t solved it here, she pointed out a funding gap. “About 3% of climate VC funding goes to water only,” she said. Water underpins industry, agriculture and now AI infrastructure, yet it remains capital-starved.

Virgovicova mentors young founders, especially women in science and climate, and her advice is very direct. “There’s always going to be skepticism in every single room you go into at first,” she said. “It’s very important that you know how to present yourself and that you’re confident. You can really prove everyone wrong as long as you know your stuff.” With women still scarce among Fortune 500 CEOs, she added, “If I can do it, you can do it as well.”

Her favorite piece of advice: “If you focus on watering your grass, you don’t care about someone’s grass being greener.” And the AI myth she wants gone? “That it’s going to destroy the world. I think it’s a tool for improving the world.”

Cisco uses this award to make a point it rarely gets credit for: technology’s value is measured by what it does for people. Xatoms applies two of the decade’s most hyped technologies, AI and quantum, to a tangible, urgent problem.

For technology leaders, there are three key takeaways. First, AI’s biggest payoff may come from scientific discovery, where compressing a decade of work into 30 days can reshape an entire industry’s economics. Second, AI’s water problem has solutions beyond cooling design, and data center builders should be evaluating treatment and reuse partners now. Third, water deserves far more capital than it receives.

In 10 years, Virgovicova wants Xatoms to be “a global leader in discovery of these materials,” with solutions for many toxic contaminants worldwide. Given how far she has come from a village of 800 people, I wouldn’t bet against her.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5577. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5576. VCs bet $30M on Larridin’s ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI’s value for money

As enterprises jack up their spending on artificial intelligence tools, it’s only right for senior executives to want to know exactly what they’re getting in return for their costly investments. Larridin Inc., a startup focused on AI adoption measurement, has just raised $30 million in early-stage funding to try to provide them with the answers.

Today’s Series A round was led by Pelion Ventures and saw participation from existing backers Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures, as well as new investors like GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital and Alumni Ventures. The round brings the company’s total amount raised so far to $47 million.

Larridin’s funding comes at a time when enterprise leaders are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value they’re getting for their spiralling token consumption costs and application programming interface bills. Shareholders of publicly traded companies, especially, are eager to see those investments are driving real growth, and aren’t easily swayed by vanity metrics showcasing adoption without value.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Russ Fradin says this pressure stems from the flawed way in which most organizations evaluate their AI investments. He argues that traditional adoption metrics such as seat licenses and login counts do not reflect the true operational impact of AI.

Indeed, one of Larridin’s own customers is a case in point. That organization’s own surveys showed that 92% of its engineers were active AI users, which seems like a good rate of adoption. But when it started using Larridin’s tools to dig deeper, it found that a single engineer accounted for 65% of the company’s entire AI budget.

These aren’t the only kinds of blind spots AI has created. In Larridin’s newly released Engineering AI Impact Report, based on a survey of more than 1,000 developers, it found that though AI-assisted pull requests increased from 35% in April to 62% in September, it didn’t provide much value for enterprises because it simply created bottlenecks further downstream. For instance, organization’s median code review wait times increased more than 50% over the same timeframe.

Fradin says this is why companies cannot just monitor AI output volume. What’s needed is a complete picture that also covers the cost and quality of AI outputs, and the friction it creates.

Larridin’s goal is to give companies more visibility into their AI technology with what it says is the industry’s first AI value measurement platform. It links data on AI tool adoption with employee productivity metrics and expenditure data, and also looks at the value generated by, and the cost of autonomous AI agents that do work on behalf of humans.

By tracking complete workflows, Larridin can help companies to identify where and how AI is actually driving value and where spend is being wasted. It can also highlight new processes that are ripe for agentic automation.

Such insights can be extremely compelling. In one case, Larridin identified a 66-fold cost discrepancy per shipped code change between two competing AI coding tools that were being used by different employees for similar tasks. The customer was able to cancel its subscription for the much more expensive tool without any impact on productivity.

“Companies must be able to prove tangible business value from skyrocketing AI spend,” Fradin said. “Our investors share that conviction, and our Series A reflects the belief in our technology and its ability to solve this critical challenge.”

Larridin’s customer base includes enterprises such as SurveyMonkey Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co., Kalviyo Inc. and Gainsight Inc., and it’s planning to build on this traction by expanding its go-to-market and engineering teams.

Pelion Ventures’ Jeff Kearl said he’s backing Larridin because it fills a vital gap in enterprise analytics by tying every dollar spent on AI directly to measurable business outcomes. “As AI adoption scales, Larridin empowers executive teams with the intelligence to maximize their return on investment and build a clear path to long-term value creation,” he said.

#5573. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5572. Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft integrate hybrid AI

How can software and cloud giant Microsoft Corp. translate its platform vision into fully deployed enterprise architecture in the age of AI?

This central question has defined the next chapter in a decades-long partnership between Microsoft and Dell Technologies Inc. Dell provided some answers at this year’s Dell Technologies World by expanding its private cloud offering to deploy the latest Microsoft software implementations.

Since that event, Microsoft has worked to enable a disaggregated architecture, simplifying operations across Dell PowerEdge compute, Dell PowerStore storage and Azure Local. Flexibility is the key attraction for enterprise customers evaluating Dell and Microsoft’s joint solutions, according to Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Microsoft and Dell are moving beyond infrastructure partnerships to deliver a more integrated go-to-market strategy for enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and application modernization,” he said. “Since Dell Technologies World in May, the focus has been on connecting Microsoft Azure Local, SQL Server and hybrid-cloud capabilities with Dell’s automation platform and enterprise infrastructure to help customers deploy, govern and operate AI workloads wherever their data resides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale,” and past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

The market opportunity for both Dell and Microsoft centers on the need to operationalize AI applications. Meeting this goal requires integration across the full AI deployment lifecycle.

Dell Automation Platform and Dell Private Cloud provide an operational backbone for deploying Azure Local on-premises and managing the hardware lifecycle, including firmware and updates. Azure Arc provides consistent management across environments. SQL Server can be run in virtual machines or Kubernetes containers without learning separate skill sets for cloud and on-premises environments.

“The key architecture for AI capabilities is integrating with things like embedding models for vector searching or chat completion models for AI agents, but we do it all inside … the SQL Server Engine,” Bob Ward, principal architect at Microsoft, told theCUBE. “We [formed a] partnership with Dell so that we can connect to anything on premises. I can connect to Azure Local, Dell [and] Nvidia Factory. We just got a framework built in. It doesn’t matter where you’re running these AI models; we can easily integrate with it.”

A central element of Dell and Microsoft’s partnership involves integrating database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a stack that can feed AI the data it needs. Data fragmentation is often cited as a top blocker to scaling AI beyond pilots, and integrating the two companies’ services addresses a pressure point that surveys have identified across enterprise information technology.

Data fragmentation remains a barrier to scaling AI beyond pilots. Dell and Microsoft’s partnership brings database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a common stack.

“From an AppDev perspective, that integration matters because the challenge is no longer simply building AI applications, but operationalizing them securely, consistently and at scale,” said Nashawaty. “TheCUBE AppDev Research highlights the execution gap: Approximately 88% of AI pilots fail to reach production, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify integration complexity as a leading barrier to adoption.”

Dell’s partnership with Microsoft also extends to unstructured data storage. The two companies are bringing familiar storage capabilities into hybrid and multicloud environments.

Dell PowerScale for Microsoft Azure brings Dell’s OneFS file system software into Azure as a managed storage service. Customers can provision file storage directly from the Azure portal while retaining familiar PowerScale management capabilities.

The solution supports a wide range of production workloads across industries. These industries increasingly depend on high-throughput, low-latency file access to drive the next generation of agentic AI and advanced analytics. Media and entertainment firms can use it to handle massive video files, real-time editing and tight production timelines. Semiconductor and electronics design houses can accelerate simulation and modeling using large datasets.

“This isn’t really about running the software just in the cloud,” said Rachna Lalwani, senior consultant, director and product manager at Dell, in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s about creating a truly integrated experience that empowers businesses to do more with their data. What they really gain is the operational consistency across their entire storage landscape.”

A recent IDC analysis found that 95% of enterprises already run at least one AI agent workflow in production, and it predicted 2.5 billion agents by 2030. With the rise of agentic AI, Dell and Microsoft are collaborating on solutions designed to help enterprises deploy autonomous agents while controlling costs.

Managing the cost of tokens, the fundamental units of data processed by large language models, is one of AI’s financial challenges. To help address it, Dell introduced Deskside Agentic AI in May in collaboration with Microsoft and Nvidia Corp., providing a local environment for building and testing AI agents.

“What’s resonating with customers right now is that the cost of tokens is through the roof,” explained Jon Siegal, senior vice president of Dell portfolio marketing at Dell. “We know even though the cost of a token has come down pretty dramatically, the amount of tokens that are being consumed right now is just astronomical. The cloud costs are just pretty high right now. How do customers balance that out and run the right workload in the right place? We’re trying to give customers a place to start. The PC is a great place to start.”

In early October, Dell announced an expansion of its Windows PCs and workstations for agentic AI. In partnership with Microsoft, Dell broadened its AI development portfolio to provide creators, developers and enterprises with more choice in how they build, test and scale agentic AI on Windows.

This marked a key step in the evolution of Windows, where the platform has evolved into a broader resource for agentic AI. Tools such as Windows AI Foundry give developers a structured path to build, package and scale agents inside a governed environment.

“With Windows, we’re going beyond just it being an operating system — we’re thinking about it as really a canvas for AI,” said Mary Ann Anderson, worldwide marketing director of Dell partnerships at Microsoft. “Pretty soon there’s going to be a point where individual employees are managing their own agents, maybe a small army of agents. You have to do that in a way that is governed and is very secure.”

Dell and Microsoft see a significant market opportunity in closing the gap between AI development and production deployment.

“Microsoft and Dell have an opportunity to address that gap by simplifying deployment, automating infrastructure operations and giving partners repeatable solutions they can take to market,” said theCUBE Research’s Nashawaty. “The real measure of success will be whether their combined ecosystem helps enterprises move from AI experimentation to production-ready applications with stronger governance, predictable costs and measurable business outcomes.”
