#5570. PagerDuty debuts Paige AI agent with renamed PD Reliability Platform and PD Labs

Operations management software company PagerDuty Inc. today introduced Paige, an artificial intelligence agent for site reliability engineering that is built to work as a member of operations and engineering teams.

Paige runs on the company’s flagship product, which as of today is called the PD Reliability Platform. Alongside both, PagerDuty opened PD Labs to put early features in front of customers while they are still being built.

The launch is aimed at a problem PagerDuty says is getting worse as AI coding tools write more production software, much of it shipped with little human review. Applications built on AI models also break in their own ways. Chief Executive John DiLullo pointed to model drift, token runaway and leaked personal data as examples. The only way to stay resilient, he said, is “to fight fire with fire, using AI itself as part of how we keep systems running.”

Customers set Paige’s permissions team by team. A team that keeps a person in the loop gets faster triage with remediation held for approval, and the agent acts on its own only in well-understood, low-risk scenarios the team has explicitly authorized. In March, PagerDuty said its SRE Agent would start joining escalation policies as a “virtual responder.” Paige, billed as the company’s next-generation SRE agent, can now be put on call that way. A lower-priority incident may never reach a human at all.

Paige’s recommendations arrive with evidence and a confidence level attached. By the time a responder reads one, many possible causes have been ruled out already. PagerDuty argues the bigger payoff comes later, once a resolved incident has been written into a shared memory that Paige consults whenever something similar fails. In a benchmark report released with the launch, the company says Paige did better than leading AI coding agents at diagnosing simulated information technology incidents.

The renamed platform, known until today as PagerDuty Operations Cloud, is where Paige gets its operational context. Incident commanders and team managers also get a new PD Reliability Platform Console, which puts incidents, on-call rotations and AI agents in one view. The console shows which agents are switched on and what each one is doing. Paige’s suggested fixes can be acted on from the same screen.

Responders can run an incident end to end in Slack or Microsoft Teams. A trigger opens a dedicated channel and a conference bridge without anyone having to set them up.

Steve Miller, director of business development at Slack, said having Paige and the platform inside Slack gives responders speed and visibility, which he called critical as “agentic and human teams operate side-by-side in the same channel.” Nobody has to write the post-incident review, which is generated as soon as the incident is resolved, and its follow-up actions come with owners and due dates already assigned.

Canadian telecommunications company Telus Corp. has wired the platform into its own centralized internal incident tool. Kulvir Gahunia, director of the Site Reliability Office at Telus, said PagerDuty’s Scribe Agent now runs through every incident, so responders “don’t have to stop and document what is happening.”

The earlier-stage work runs through PD Labs, which PagerDuty is building in the open with design partners who get early access and a direct line to the engineers writing the code.

Three experiments are in preview to start. Topology keeps a live map of an organization’s services, assembled from its code, infrastructure and runbooks. No configuration management database is needed, and the map scopes the blast radius of a problem automatically as conditions change.

Deep Investigation has Paige test several root-cause hypotheses at once while showing its reasoning on each as new evidence comes in. SRE Workbench gives people and agents one workspace to tackle a problem side by side, and whatever they find is saved to the same memory Paige learns from.

IT teams want measurable results from their spending on AI agents, according to Snow Tempest, research manager for IT service management at International Data Corp. Better uptime counts, as does time handed back to responders who would otherwise be “chasing logs and assembling the right people for an incident.” More organizations also want to prevent incidents, Tempest said.

Paige and the PD Reliability Platform are generally available today, and SRE Workbench is open to try through PD Labs. The platform is sold for a fee tied to operational scale that comes with a starting allotment of ingested events, automation actions and user seats. Customers who outgrow it can buy flexible credits without having to forecast usage ahead of time.

#5567. Startup Athena raises $2.5M in pre-seed funding to revamp the revenue model for legal AI

Athena Circle Corp., an artificial intelligence-native legal technology startup that’s automating the nitty gritty of commercial real estate deals, said today it has raised $2.5 million in pre-seed funding.

The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz’s accelerator program, a16z Speedrun. No other investors were named.

Legal AI technology is nothing new, but its adoption in the industry has been somewhat haphazard, for the technology has exposed an awkward problem: Most law firms are still billing their clients by the hour, and that makes automation less lucrative. If a law firm can use AI agents to get a 10-hour contract review done in just a couple of minutes, then it’s going to let an awful lot of billable revenue slip through its fingers, killing any incentive there might be to adopt them.

Athena’s co-founders Cem Ucan (pictured, left) and Kieran John Keenan (right) and founding engineer José Braz all cut their teeth at the pioneering legal AI tech startup Legora AB, where they quickly realized how AI conflicts with the industry’s standard business model. They came up with an entirely different business model to convince legal firms of the benefits of automation. Instead of selling software tools directly, it provides a legal service through its affiliated law firm, charging a fixed fee per transaction that’s typically 30% to 50% lower than standard rates. In this way, it ensures that revenue is better aligned with efficiency.

“Most legal AI companies sell tools to traditional law firms, but we took a different approach,” Ucan said. “Our AI works hand-in-hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that actually move deals forward.”

The startup is focused on automating the intricacies of commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing. Its AI agents are designed to automate the creation and review of purchase agreements and loan documents, and will handle all of the due diligence and administrative closing hurdles needed to get deals done, while ensuring human lawyers remain fully in the loop to make all of the final legal determinations.

In this way, Athena basically takes care of the grunt work, giving commercial real estate firms much more agility. That’s a real advantage, because commercial real estate is an industry where speed is of the essence: The faster a law firm gets things done, the more likely it is to actually secure the deal, which is the end result that everyone wants. With investors often submitting dozens of bids for each property listing, the ability to get the paperwork done in a matter of hours rather than weeks or days means buyers can lock in a deal before their rivals know what’s happened.

Keenan, who serves as the startup’s chief technology officer, explained that each new workflow begins with an incoming agreement that’s ingested by its AI agents. They cross-reference the terms of the deal against their standard deal sheets in order to flag inconsistencies, prepare redlines and draft client communications.

This work is informed by historical transactions, which allow its agents to adapt to each client’s negotiating style, Keenan said. Human attorneys then review this work, make strategic judgment calls when required, and approve all deliverables before they’re sent to clients.

“I measure our progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent’s work and confidently stand behind it,” Keenan explained. “A draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Making that review more efficient is how our platform helps us deliver faster legal services with the quality clients expect.”

Athena’s agents are already proving their worth, with the startup having signed up 22 legal firms as clients so far, just two months after launching its service. By learning continuously from attorney’s edits and client’s preferences, its agents have reduced review times by an average of 70%.

L. Miguel Arce, chief executive of the Texas-based multifamily real estate and property management firm Mox Living, said Athena was able to deliver a complete purchase agreement in less than 48 hours, the fastest turnaround he has ever seen. “A lot of firms in our industry have an AI task force in name only,” he said. “What stood out about Athena is that the system learns from every deal, from what the attorneys change to what we prefer. Speed only matters if it’s quality work, and Athena gets us both.”

Keenan said Athena is primed to strike while the iron is hot. He said the industry is bracing itself for a wave of new commercial deals as properties financed through short-term loans in 2021 and 2022 hit their refinancing deadlines, and he’s hoping that the startup can win a significant amount of that business. In any case, growth is on the horizon, for Athena also plans to expand into new markets and property classes and even new legal domains.

A16z Speedrun’s Troy Kirwin said AI automation is all well and good, but clients still demand to speak to a human who can take responsibility for the work that gets done. “Athena is building around that need with a system that can improve through real legal work and a team that’s obsessed with scaling fast,” he said.

#5564. Exclusive: Cogent Security’s VR-1.1 model outscores Claude Code and Codex on vulnerability repair

Vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today released VR-1.1, a new version of its frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.

On a public repair benchmark, the model outscored Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex.

The release goes after the part of vulnerability management that has not sped up. In July, research group Epoch Artificial Intelligence Inc. counted about 2,500 high- and critical-severity disclosures from major organizations, roughly five times the monthly record set before Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview in April.

Each repair still needs an engineer who understands the flaw well enough to change the code without breaking something else. Co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti called that stage “where security teams are stuck.”

To test the model on that repair work, Cogent turned to LiveCVEBench. Researchers at Harbin Institute of Technology and Kuaishou Technology built the benchmark from vulnerabilities disclosed in recent months and add new ones regularly. VR-1.1 produced a working repair for 57.9% of the benchmark’s 190 tasks. Claude Code and Codex tied at 45.3%.

Each task drops an agent into a real development environment with a vulnerability report and the affected codebase, in one of 14 programming languages. To pass, a patch has to close the vulnerability without breaking the software, which the benchmark checks with separate security and functionality tests.

Cogent blocked outbound network access during repairs and hid the grading tests until each agent was done. Inference budgets differed across the three systems, according to the full methodology Cogent Research has published.

Where the environment allows, VR-1.1 starts by writing its own proof of concept that triggers the reported flaw. From there the model follows the vulnerability through the affected code, including related paths that share the same weakness. The fix itself stays small, for example checking an index before use.

Every patch goes to a separate review that starts from a fresh context and hunts for a way around the fix. New bugs introduced by the change are part of that check. The model also leaves behind regression tests, which fail if a later code change reopens the flaw. When an attempt fails, the diagnosis and failure details carry into the next try.

“A patch might block the exact payload from a bug report, but leave the same vulnerability open via a different endpoint or break core functionality for users,” said Geng Sng, co-founder and chief technology officer of Cogent. “We designed VR-1.1 to check its own work for both problems before it finishes.”

Cogent introduced VR-1 in July to find and prove the attack paths an adversary could reach inside an enterprise. The new release extends the remediation capabilities that model introduced.

Founded in 2025, the company sells artificial intelligence agents that detect and fix vulnerabilities, with customers choosing whether a human signs off on each change. According to Cogent, Fortune 500 users have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%.

Greylock Partners backed its $11 million launch round in July 2025, and Bain Capital Ventures led the $42 million Series A in February that took total funding to $53 million.

#5561. Novee’s External Surface Testing checks which exposed assets attackers can actually exploit

Artificial intelligence penetration testing startup Novee Cyber Security Ltd. today added External Surface Testing to its platform so its AI-driven attacks can reach a customer’s entire internet-facing footprint.

External Surface Testing is aimed at the scramble after a critical vulnerability is disclosed, when security teams have to work out which exposed assets are affected and whether any can actually be exploited. Novee argues that attackers see a target as a single environment with many ways in, including forgotten subdomains and staging servers someone left exposed.

Conventional external attack surface management products catalog a company’s exposed assets and score them by severity. Netta Rager Dan, vice president of product at Novee, said those products “show you what’s exposed, but don’t give you the full picture of real risk.” In the company’s telling, security staff are left to validate long lists of exposures on their own.

Novee’s version needs nothing more than a domain name to get started. From there the software works outward the way an outside attacker would, and it keeps track of what it learns about each asset and service as it goes. A newly disclosed vulnerability gets run against a customer’s live systems to see whether anyone could actually exploit it.

Findings exported from other vendors’ attack surface tools go through the same check. Novee says the testing also catches flaws nobody had logged, chained attack paths among them, and the customer ends up with a short, prioritized list of validated issues backed by evidence.

Until now Novee’s testing has stopped at the application layer. External Surface Testing runs on the same platform as the company’s Application Pentesting product, so a host found during external discovery can be promoted straight into a full gray-box or white-box pentest. Whatever the discovery phase learned carries over. Novee claims no other fully autonomous AI pentesting platform covers the external attack surface as well as web, mobile and AI applications.

Limits are built in to keep the testing safe. Customers approve the scope before anything runs, and the probes come from outside the perimeter without agents or customer-supplied credentials. Exploit attempts don’t use destructive payloads. Traffic is held under configured caps so testing doesn’t cause load spikes or bury the security operations center in noise.

Former national-level offensive security operators Ido Geffen, Gon Chalamish and Omer Ninburg founded Novee in May 2025. YL Ventures LP, Canaan Partners and Zeev Ventures LP backed the company when it launched in January with $51.5 million in funding.

External Surface Testing is available now as part of the Novee platform.

#5560. The concessions field problem that breaks pay-for-listing data models

Contribution schemes that credit MLS data by listing totals overlook whether key valuation inputs are complete. A single MLS can require a numeric concessions amount whenever concessions are yes, improving downstream appraisal and model reliability.  AI Summary

Metering who uses listing data is an engineering problem with engineering answers. Deciding what a contributed listing is worth is not, and the difficulty sits in the field definitions rather than in anybody’s policy.

The proposal itself is sound, and it is gaining ground. Meter extraction, credit the organizations that supply the data, and reward the brokerages that send more of their eligible inventory into the system rather than less. Paper agreements stop working the moment data leaves the system, and an incentive attached to the record travels wherever the record goes.A contribution model based primarily on listing counts risks rewarding volume rather than the completeness and usefulness of the information. That is the obvious unit, and it is the wrong one, because two listings entered on the same morning by the same brokerage can differ by the only thing a valuation needs.

The RESO Data Dictionary permits three answers to whether a closed sale carried concessions: yes, no and call listing agent. The ‘Concessions Amount’ sits beside it as a number field, ‘Concessions Comments’ as free text. All three belong to the closing group, which RESO describes as intended to describe facts that occurred at the closing of a transaction rather than offers made before it. RESO’s own guidance says recording this data consistently is important, and notes that adopting the newer concessions fields is optional for any organization.A concession is consideration. Fannie Mae specifically says concessions adjustments should reflect their impact on the transaction price, rather than automatically deducting the full dollar amount of concessions. In some cases, the market-based adjustment may be smaller than the concession or unnecessary. Also, RESO’s concessions fields for closed transactions shouldn’t be confused with fields advertising potential seller concessions before closing.

RESO explicitly distinguishes the two uses in its April 2024 guidance. It moves the figure a buyer paid without moving the figure the deed records, and that gap is the entire reason an appraiser adjusts for it. Fannie Mae requires adjustments to reflect the market’s reaction to the difference between properties, naming paired sales as one method among statistical analysis, modeling and other commonly accepted approaches. Every one of them needs the magnitude.

It is not one field. View carries 38 category words, among them ‘Bay’, ‘City Lights’, ‘Ocean’ and ‘Panoramic’, with no amount and no rating attached. ‘Entry Level’ carries the floor as a number and nothing joins the two, while Fannie Mae’s condo section requires special attention to a unit’s location within its project and says nothing about view at all.So, a contribution model priced by record count pays for the half of the work that costs nothing. An address, bedrooms, bathrooms and a price make a record. The concession amount, the extent of the view and the condition detail make it evidence. Paying the same for both, or partial credit for the thinner one, is a reliable way to end up with more records rather than better ones.

I think requiring a number whenever the answer to the concessions question is ‘yes’ is a rules change inside a single MLS’s authority, enforceable at the point of entry, and it costs an agent the half minute it takes to read a closing statement already in front of them. Apply it to the other fields that carry magnitude rather than category and a contribution model has something worth metering.The alternative is a market that pays for volume. Records multiply, credits clear and the fields that decide what a house is worth carry whatever they happen to carry, because nothing in the scheme ever asked for them.The governance conversation is about who may read the record. What the record contains is a separate question, and it is the one that can be answered this quarter by any organization willing to make a single field mandatory.Nikola Gojkovic is the founder of CMAflow and writes on residential valuation methodology.

#5559. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5557. RealTrends Verified brokerage ERA Live Moore acquisition and other brokerage moves

Several brokerages announced acquisitions and affiliations across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic. Highlights include ERA Live Moore’s Blue Door Group deal, SERHANT.’s Pennsylvania leadership hire, and expansions by Corcoran Reverie and Century 21.  AI Summary

ERA Live Moore, one of the Carolinas’ premier real estate brokerages, today announced the acquisition of Blue Door Group Real Estate, a respected and established local firm serving the Greater Winston Salem market. Moving forward, the brokerage will operate as Blue Door Group Real Estate, an ERA Live Moore Company, preserving its trusted local identity while connecting agents and clients to the expanded resources of the ERA Live Moore network.

Blue Door Group Real Estate was founded in 2020 by Jodi Tate, who is no stranger to ERA Live Moore: in 2016, ERA Live Moore owner Eb hand-picked her to launch their Winston Salem office, knowing that one day she wanted to establish her own company. After significantly expanding the ERA office’s agent base, she started Blue Door group in 2020 with Eb and Tania’s full support.

RealTrends Verified brokerage SERHANT. announced the appointment of Mishel Taylor as Managing Director and Principal Broker of SERHANT. Pennsylvania. A licensed broker in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, Taylor joins from eXp Realty, LLC and brings more than two decades of experience spanning residential finance, multi-office brokerage management, agent development, and organizational growth across the New Jersey and Greater Philadelphia region.

In her new role, Taylor will oversee brokerage operations, compliance, recruiting and agent performance for SERHANT. Pennsylvania. She will focus on building scalable systems that help agents grow their businesses across Philadelphia’s city neighborhoods and the Main Line communities, from Center City to Bryn Mawr, Villanova and Wayne.

Corcoran Reverie, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, announced its acquisition of NextHome Music City Realty, expanding the firm’s presence across Tennessee. The Murfreesboro-based brokerage will now operate under the Corcoran Reverie banner. Co-owners Tad Ritchison and Todd Grubaugh will continue to lead their team of agents and serve clients throughout Nashville, Franklin, Murfreesboro and the surrounding communities.

Century 21 Real Estate LLC, which has franchises recognized on the RealTrends Verified top brokerage list, is expanding its brand presence along Florida’s Atlantic coast with the latest affiliation of Realty Exchange LLC, a 20-year-old brokerage with nearly 100 independent sales professionals based in Palm Coast.

Now doing business as CENTURY 21 Realty Exchange, the brokerage was founded in 2006 by Julie Sabine, who continues to lead the business alongside co-owner Dave Petkovsek. Sabine, a full-time real estate professional since 2004, has helped close over 1,600 transactions across her 22-year career.

RealTrends Verified brokerage Michael Saunders & Company, announced that the commercial real estate team and business operations of Florida ROI Commercial Property Brokerage, a Tampa-based firm established in 2008, have transitioned to its commercial division, MSC Commercial. As part of the transition, the property portfolio previously managed by Florida Investment Real Estate (FIRE) will also move to MSC Commercial, extending its presence into the greater Tampa Bay market.

The move builds on Michael Saunders & Company’s recent expansion into Sanibel Island and Pinellas County/St. Petersburg and marks another significant step in the company’s continued growth up and down Florida’s Gulf Coast, where the firm’s offices, listings, and market experience now extend from Tampa Bay to Fort Myers.

#5556. Groundcover turns its Wand acquisition into a Kubernetes rightsizing beta

Observability company groundcover Inc. today added Autonomous Infrastructure to its platform in beta to rightsize the processor and memory requests automatically on customers’ Kubernetes workloads based on how each workload behaves in production.

The technology comes from Kubernetes resource optimization startup Wand Cloud Ltd., which groundcover acquired in September.

The release is aimed at the processor and memory requests Kubernetes has engineers set for each workload up front, usually before it has handled any real traffic, and groundcover said most teams seldom return to those numbers. When one is set too low, the first sign is often a service throwing out-of-memory errors. Padding that goes unused ends up on the monthly cloud bill.

Because the groundcover sensor has been collecting production history all along, a customer on a supported version can open Autonomous Infrastructure for the first time without installing anything and find the data the feature needs already in place. Requested processor and memory for each workload appear next to actual usage. Estimated monthly savings sit beside a count of under-provisioned workloads, and a chart tracks over time how much of the potential saving has been realized.

Dollar figures in the beta are based on a price per processor and memory unit that customers enter themselves. Public cloud pricing is the next step, according to groundcover, and billing data such as the Cost and Usage Report from Amazon Web Services Inc. will come after that.

Most resource optimization tools size each workload in isolation, groundcover argues, so a request that looks right for one service can still starve its neighbors on a crowded node. Stability is the first constraint in groundcover’s own software. Before Autonomous Infrastructure raises a request, it checks how tightly the node is already packed so one workload’s increase does not leave the rest short of resources.

Shahar Azulay, groundcover’s co-founder and chief executive, said customers can check what their clusters stand to save, from data already held in their own cloud accounts, before they let Autonomous Infrastructure “change anything.” The feature stays off until an engineer turns it on and picks the deployments, namespaces or clusters it manages.

During the beta the software touches requests only and leaves limits where they are. Each policy carries minimum and maximum bounds for processor and memory, and an audit log records who assigned each workload to a policy and when. Groundcover suggests starting with lower-risk workloads such as development namespaces and leaving alone something like a production database that needs room to grow.

The beta is available now at no additional cost to every groundcover customer running its sensor on Kubernetes, and the company is also recruiting design partners to work with its product team while it runs. Demonstrations are scheduled for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City Nov. 9-12.

Groundcover is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $160 million to date, including a $100 million Series C round led by One Peak in July.

#5555. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5554. Why Offerpad is getting more selective on home buys

Offerpad said faster rising mortgage rates and affordability pressures slowed home sales in Q3 2026. The iBuyer tightened acquisition criteria, leaned more on brokerage and its marketplace and guided to positive adjusted EBITDA run rate by Q2 2027.  AI Summary

Heading into the second half of 2026, Offerpad was laser-focused on “turning its buying engine back on,” however, housing market headwinds caused by rapidly rising mortgage rates and continued affordability challenges, have led the iBuyer to increase the intentionality behind its strategy.

In a call with investors and analysts to discuss the company’s third quarter 2026 earnings, Offerpad executives said that with homes taking longer to sell, the firm adjusted its acquisition criteria to require higher expected returns on a property. In addition, they said the company has become more selective about new purchases and that it adjusted its underwriting to build wider expected margins into each purchase.

Instead of providing home sellers with a direct cash offer, executives said Offerpad was looking to serve more sellers through its Cash Offer Marketplace and Brokerage Services offerings.

During the quarter, Offerpad recorded 324 total transactions, up from 295 transactions a quarter prior, but down 32% annually. Executives attributed the lower-than-anticipated number of transactions for the quarter to the overall slower housing market.

“We’ve operated with mortgage rates above 7% before,” Brian Bair, the CEO of Offerpad, said during the earnings call Monday evening. “What was different this time was the speed of the move late in our quarter and the attention it received. Housing affordability has become a national story. With headlines describing it as a buyer’s market. Buyers weighed higher monthly payments against the possibility of a better deal. While sellers faced uncertainty about how long their homes would take to sell and what price they could achieve. We believe that combination contributed to a more cautious market as the quarter came to a close.”

In total, Offerpad’s Brokerage Services and Cash Offer Marketplace represented approximately 35% of Q3 closed transactions, with the company noting that brokerage listing signings more than doubled from Q2 2026.

In total, Offerpad acquired 605 homes during the quarter, up 198% annually. According to executives, these purchases were concentrated in markets where homes were still selling at a pace that met the company’s requirements. On the sales side, Offerpad sold 210 homes during the quarter, down 43% annually, but up slightly from Q2 2026.

“Last quarter, we said we were increasing acquisitions and we did by acquiring 605 homes in Q3. We also had additional homes under contract that could have increased that total. As market conditions shifted, we reevaluated them against our wider margin requirements and chose not to proceed with homes that no longer met our criteria,” Bair, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said. “Where possible, we offered those sellers an alternative through cash offer or broker services. Buying well is only half the process.”

At the end of the quarter aged inventory represented just 2.6% of all homes on the balance sheet, well below Offerpad’s 10% aged inventory threshold. The company said that this inventory is expected to provide a pipeline of dispositions through the rest of 2026 and into early 2027. So far in Q4, leaders said 200 homes have sold or are under contract for sale.

Bair noted on the call that Offerpad’s current portfolio of homes is “healthy” and that most were bought within the last few months.

Looking ahead, Offerpad executives said that returning to profitability is the company’s primary focus. During the third quarter of 2026, Offerpad recorded $78.1 million in revenue, down 41% annually, while the company’s net loss of $11.5 million for the quarter was a 1% improvement compared to a year prior. As the iBuyer looks to get back into the black, executives said they are focused on reducing operating expenses and growing Cash Offer Marketplace and brokerage services.

While the company has cut operating expenses by more than $140 million since 2022, during Q3, executives said they identified an additional $8 million to $10 million in annualized operating expense reductions, which they expect to be implemented in 2027.

“Profitability remains our No. 1 priority. And nothing about that has changed. What has changed is the timeline. The shift in the market has pushed our path out, and we now expect to exit the second quarter of 2027 at a positive adjusted EBITDA run rate,” Bair said. “Together, these actions give us the opportunity to reach positive adjusted EBITDA with fewer transactions than before.”

Offerpad executives have noted that they believe positive adjusted EBITDA will come with roughly 1,000 transactions per quarter. In Q4 2026, the company said it anticipated 400-475 transactions, but executives are optimistic the firm will reach that 1,000 transaction threshold. On the call, executives noted that the firm is using lenders to fund a larger share of each home’s cost, meaning that less of Offerpad’s capital is tied up in the homes the firm buys.

“That makes our capital go further and it helps it return to the business faster as homes sell. At quarter end, we had approximately $251 million of undrawn capacity under our inventory financing facilities, the majority of which is uncommitted,” Andrew Piper, who was appointed interim chief financial officer, replacing Peter Knag, said. “We believe our cash, the capital we expect to return as homes sell, and our inventory financing are sufficient as we execute our 2027 plan. We also remain open to opportunities to strengthen our balance sheet, including strategic capital partnerships, and we will be disciplined about the structure and cost of any capital we add.”

#5552. Snowflake expands agentic AI platform with business context and governance tools

Snowflake Inc. today announced a sweeping collection of artificial intelligence capabilities designed to bring business context, governance and autonomous development into the same environment, as enterprises increasingly hand over software engineering and everyday operations to AI agents.

The announcements, during the company’s Expedition 2026 virtual conference, include a new Business Ontology framework, expanded agent governance through Cortex AI Gateway, and autonomous data engineering capabilities that allow AI agents to build, monitor and troubleshoot data pipelines with less human intervention.

The company is betting that more coders and engineers will use AI throughout the software development lifecycle as creation moves even faster, while other back-end departments begin to adopt agents in their day-to-day work. For example, sales operations are creating agents that can analyze sales risks and prepare customer outreach without writing code.

“AI is industrializing software creation. Actually, it’s industrializing intelligence,” Chief Executive Sridhar Ramaswamy said. “What once took months can now take hours, days, or even minutes.”

Ramaswamy noted that while AI is changing the economics of software development, as agents take over tasks usually relegated to specialized developers, business users become developers. This is changing the competitive landscape, meaning that the advantage no longer goes to specialists, but to proprietary knowledge.

Snowflake is taking the field by helping ordinary AI models understand and contextualize that business knowledge. It does this with Business Ontology, an extension of its existing semantic views that lets organizations establish approved definitions used across the organization. Without a standard definition, two agents could respond to the same business-related question with incompatible answers, even when both agents have accurate underlying data.

Using information from Business Ontology, Snowflake CoCo, the coding agent for data teams, and Snowflake CoWork, the personal work agent for knowledge workers, use these approved business concepts to ground their responses.

This new feature is currently in private preview, but is headed to public preview soon.

Cortex AI Gateway arrives to become a single front door for agents within an organization. It is not entirely new; Snowflake introduced it in July 2026 as a centralized way to govern and monitor agents.

Today’s announcement expands its capabilities rather than introducing the gateway for the first time. The new updates include agent abuse detection, observability and tracing, Cortex sandboxes, AI cost governance, dynamic model routing and tools integration using technology from Snowflake’s Natoma acquisition.

“An agent that acts on your business has to be trusted, and it has to know three important things: what the data means, which data to trust, and what it’s allowed to do,” said Ramaswamy.

The platform most importantly applies existing security mechanisms, including data masking and access restrictions, to agent-driven operations while adding capabilities to monitor activity, detect potential abuse and maintain records of what agents do. The information technology and security teams can also apply cost controls, select models based on efficiency or accuracy and restrict which external tools agents can access granularly.

The underlying role of this governance, control and transparency is aligned with giving agents the same sort of role observation granted to employees. Treating them similarly in terms of autonomy.

Snowflake’s push comes amid a broader industry race to establish the control layer for enterprise AI agents. SAP has been expanding its Autonomous Enterprise architecture and governed Joule agents, while Salesforce has introduced its Enterprise AI Harness and AI Control Plane to secure autonomous workflows. Snowflake is approaching the same problem from the data platform side, seeking to become the foundation through which agents access trusted business information and operate under enterprise policies.

Snowflake also announced the public preview of Cortex Training, which will allow customers to tailor open-weight AI models with their own proprietary information.

The service is designed to make it simpler to create specialized models using post-training without needing vast arrays of graphics processing units. Snowflake lets them train models without managing the underlying infrastructure.

“Specialized, smaller models that come with more efficient responses, faster responses, and frequently cost benefits in terms of tokens,” Executive Vice President of Product Christian Kleinerman said.

Many enterprise companies will require sovereign control of their own AI models as increasing restrictions on foreign open-weight AI or regulations on handling sensitive information. It’s easier to audit what passes through an AI model on your own hardware than in a third-party vendor’s cloud.

Separately, Snowflake announced an expanded partnership with Oracle Corp. to make its platform available as a first-party service on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The integration will give customers easier access to Snowflake’s analytics and AI capabilities while allowing them to work directly through Oracle databases and applications.

#5551. Mortgage rates have a quiet week as markets digest Fed comments, Trump’s directive

Mortgage rates were mostly flat week over week, with the 30-year fixed averaging 7.38%. Jumbo and FHA rates fell modestly, while markets are still pricing a likely 25-bps Fed hike in December.  AI Summary

Mortgage rate movement was largely flat in the past week, with the downward momentum of previous weeks cooling off even as more potential homebuyers have been incentivized to seek financing.

At HousingWire’s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year loans averaged 7.38% — the same as one week ago. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans averaged 7.62%, down 7 bps in a week, while 30-year rates for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans stood at 7.16%, down 8 bps.

The small declines in rates come a week after the Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate at a range of 3.75% of 4% in a widely expected decision. But after policymakers hiked rates in September, further increases are anticipated, with the CME Group’s FedWatch tool showing that 77% of interest rate traders predict a 25-basis-point increase in December.

HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami wrote this week that tighter monetary policy “has created financial pain for some AI companies.” With the Fed focusing on the inflationary aspects of AI and associated debt-financing issues, the 10-year Treasury yield has been dropping, which has placed downward pressure on mortgage rates.

Hector Amendola, president of Las Vegas-based mortgage lender SimplyPMG, told HousingWire in an interview that he believes a December hike is already baked into current rates and that drastic movement, up or down, is unlikely to happen for the rest of this year.

“It’s kind of been par for the course now for a while, that rates are continuing to rise based on the expectation that the Fed will go up a little bit more until there’s a way to figure out how to tame inflation a little bit,” Amendola said.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced last week that the central bank would be shifting to fewer policy votes in each of the next two years. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) currently meets eight times a year, with a vote scheduled after each, but the number of votes will be reduced to seven in 2027 and potentially to six in 2028.

“I think it puts a little bit more weight on each of the meetings,” he said. “I also think it’s interesting, because as Warsh kicks over, you’re kind of wondering if it’ll be like, ‘Let’s break everything and see what happens and figure it out later,’ or are we going to continue to really look at the data and do what the data tells us?

“I think what I’ve seen so far is, it’s still a wait-and-see approach. Let’s see what the data says, and that’s kind of why I think this particular decision that came out [last week] was expected, because the data is saying, ‘Slow down.’”

Last month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that targets lower costs in multiple areas of housing finance. These include proactive mortgage insurance cancellations for conventional loan servicers, an expanded title waiver program through the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), reduced rates on some government-backed loans and the creation of a manufactured housing task force.

Mat Ishbia, president and CEO of United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), said this week in his monthly “3 Points” video that “housing affordability continues to be front and center in Washington D.C. There’s a real focus right now on finding ways to lower the cost of homeownership, reduce friction in the mortgage process and make financing more accessible.”

He pointed specifically to the proposal to make the title insurance waiver pilot a permanent program, saying that prior waivers on some low-risk refinances have been “saving consumers thousands of dollars.”

“Some of these ideas will help; some of them won’t help,” Ishbia said of the executive order. “We’ll see how it all shakes out. But I think these are good things they’re looking at doing.”

Amendola said his company has “always been big proponents” of waiving title insurance on refi transactions with loan-to-value ratios below 80%. “Like, what are we really doing? It’s the same consumer. You know, all that stuff is still coming up,” he remarked.

He also said that allowing servicers of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans to help borrowers cancel their mortgage insurance premiums when they reach the statutory threshold “is a bigger deal than people think.” U.S. Mortgage Insurers have expressed their support for the move, while some analysts label it as “fairly benign” for the financial performance of mortgage insurers.

“That’s extra revenue that they’re making right now that they, honestly, probably shouldn’t be making — and suddenly they’re going to have an impact on their end,” Amendola said. “But it’s going to be really good for the homeowner to free up some of that cash that can then turn into something else for them.”

Fractal Q2 Net Income Jumps 139% on revenue growth of 20%

NEW YORK, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fractal Analytics Ltd (BSE: 544700) (NSE: FRACTAL), an enterprise AI company that builds its own AI models, platforms and products for Fortune 500Â® organizations, announced its consolidated financial results for Q2 FY27, ending September 30, 2026.

In Q2 FY27, the Company reported consolidated operating revenue of INR 9,565 m, a growth of 20% year on year (YoY) and 10% in constant currency terms YoY. Revenue growth was led by the company's Healthcare and Life Sciences (HLS) industry, which clocked 79% growth YoY. Banking, Financial Services and Insurance (BFSI) also performed very well, growing 30% YoY in Q2 and the company has delivered strong sustained growth in HLS and BFSI over the last several quarters. Fractal's largest industry vertical, Consumer Packaged Goods and Retail (CPGR), grew 11% YoY. TMT saw strong sequential recovery with 6% QoQ growth. Fractal's products, including the Cogentiq agentic AI platform, reached an annual revenue run-rate of over INR 1,500 m, up 39% YoY.

#5549. LiveX brings engaging, AI-powered intelligent human-sized avatar kiosks to retail and airport sites

Palo Alto-based LiveX AI Inc., a company building interactive experience artificial intelligence agents for retail and hospitality environments, today announced AI City, its kiosk-driven, life-size, human-like AI hosts.

The company’s products, currently deployed in more than 100 sites, engage guests through life-sized human avatars across retail, technology, hospitality and entertainment. Customer sites include PUMA stores, San José Mineta International Airport, SAP Center, the San Jose Sharks stadium, El Camino Hospital, and Marriott and Hilton hotels.

“We believe intelligence of this nature should meet people wherever they are, live and in person, where life happens,” said President and Chief AI Officer Jia Li. “AI should be greeting travelers at the airport, guiding a grandmother through the hospital, helping every shopper like the best employee in the building or answering sixty thousand fans at once.”

A traditional interactive kiosk relies on rigid menus and doesn’t converse with the user; it also doesn’t automatically translate into the user’s native language by simply listening to them speak. An AI City kiosk can see and hear the other person and react almost like another person, using real-time discovery to provide personalized help.

The company added that these kiosks are coming as companies try to bring other physical AI products, such as general-purpose robotics, to market, but these are still years away from widespread deployment.

As a kiosk, a user could walk up and see a projected AI person who can assist with navigation, product recommendations, event guidance or answer questions about the venue. According to LiveX, the City kiosk products have been expanded with interactive 3D maps for location-aware navigation and discovery, 3D products and multilingual translation.

LiveX said such a system could assist customers with product, venue and event questions, enabling staff to walk around with more customers at the site and handle more complex problems requiring deeper oversight.

“AI that can understand people and their surroundings is opening new ways to make everyday spaces more helpful and accessible,” said Madison Huang, senior director of product marketing for physical AI at Nvidia Corp.

The LiveX Interactive Intelligence platform runs on Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition graphics processing units and uses the Metropolis VSS Blueprint to build visual AI agents powered by Nvidia Cosmos, an open world model builder. Nvidia also provided a surface for supplying libraries from Omniverse, which delivers digital twins for location-aware applications.

LiveX said its platform brings together proprietary models it developed and trained for human interaction, shaped on real-world interaction data and experience through live deployments. Its Omni Model provides multimodal understanding and responses, while a noise management model lets it assist users even with significant background noise.

#5548. Real Brokerage expands in Midwest with Iowa-based The Team

The Real Brokerage announced that Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit moved their 30-agent group, The Team, to Real. The Dubuque, Iowa-based brokerage covers Iowa, Illinois and Wisconsin, with reported volume of $1.2B since 2020.  AI Summary

The Real Brokerage announced that real estate leaders Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit have moved their 30-agent brokerage to Real under the name The Team. The group, based in Dubuque, Iowa, previously operated as an independent brokerage known as Unlimited.

The Team serves buyers and sellers across Dubuque; Galena, Illinois; and southern Wisconsin. Since 2020, the brokerage has closed about 5,000 transactions totaling $1.2 billion in volume, according to the company announcement.

The move gives Real, a top-ranked firm by RealTrends Verified, a larger foothold in a smaller but active Midwest market as national brokerages continue to compete for productive teams rather than individual agents. For brokers and team leaders, these platform moves can signal shifting economics around splits, stock incentives, technology stacks and administrative support.

Buchheit brings more than 30 years of real estate experience to Real and also co-owns multiple complementary businesses in property management, insurance, HVAC, cleaning and construction. That ecosystem can create cross-sales and referral opportunities while helping to stabilize revenue through market cycles.

Buchheit recruited Burger to Unlimited in 2020 to run the company, a partnership that preceded Unlimited’s merger with the region’s largest brokerage. Together they grew Unlimited into a local market leader by both agent count and production, the announcement explained.

Burger has balanced ownership responsibilities with active production. He is on track to generate about $15 million in personal sales volume in 2026, according to the announcement.

At Real, Burger and Buchheit plan to leverage the firm’s cloud-based brokerage platform to streamline operations, recruit additional agents and expand into new Midwest markets.

“Cody and Dennis have built a business with a strong regional presence and a clear vision for growth,” Joel Kirsch, senior vice president of growth at Real and a 2024 HousingWire Insider, said in the announcement. “They bring valuable operational experience, production success and an entrepreneurial mindset.”

Buchheit said the switch was driven largely by technology and long-term positioning.

“Real is light-years ahead when it comes to technology and where the industry is going,” he said, noting that the platform and community provide tools and relationships to “build a business that’s positioned for the future.”

Burger said the move will allow him to spend less time on day-to-day management and more time on production, agent development and geographic expansion. “I’ve spent years running every aspect of the business while still producing, and Real gives me an opportunity to take a lot off my plate,” he said.

#5547. /C O R R E C T I O N - Chord/

In the news release, Chord Expands into Enterprise AI With Zenlytic Acquisition, Adding Verizon, J.Crew, Domino's, and Stanley Black & Decker as Customers, issued 03-Nov-2026 by Chord over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

NEW YORK, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Chord, the AI native data platform for commerce, announced its acquisition of Zenlytic, an AI-powered business intelligence platform, doubling its revenue and adding a customer portfolio that includes Verizon, J.Crew, Domino's, and Stanley Black & Decker.

The acquisition accelerates Chord's expansion beyond commerce brands to address a growing challenge in enterprise businesses: giving agents access to data is easier than ensuring they understand the business. As definitions, metrics, and financial goals change, Chord keeps that context current, enforces permissions, and gives companies oversight of the answers their agents produce as AI scales across teams.

This was a strategic acquisition as Chord and Zenlytic went to market to solve the same problem: making AI reliable on company data. Chord built an end-to-end context layer for commerce brands, while Zenlytic developed an approach that works across industries on existing enterprise data warehouses. Bringing Zenlytic's technology and key team members into Chord accelerates that shared mission, helping more companies adopt and scale AI across the organization.

As AI becomes central to how enterprises and brands operate, companies need a reliable way to move from individual experiments to agents that work across the business. Without shared definitions and controls, teams can receive conflicting answers from the same data, spend time verifying results, and struggle to turn AI adoption into measurable business value.

"As enterprises and commerce brands make AI core to their operations, they're facing a critical decision about who controls the data and knowledge that make their businesses unique," said Bryan Mahoney, co-founder and CEO of Chord. "We saw what happened in commerce when brands became dependent on Facebook and Google to reach their own customers. Now, as OpenAI and Anthropic become central to how businesses use AI, there's a risk of repeating that same dependency with enterprise data and intelligence. Companies shouldn't have to hand over control of their most valuable business context to benefit from AI. Bringing Zenlytic into Chord gives them the infrastructure to own that context, keep it current, and use it across whichever AI models they choose."

Chord addresses this data challenge by giving teams and agents a shared, governed understanding of the business that stays current as it changes. This foundation helps companies expand AI across functions while retaining control of their data and the flexibility to adopt new models as the technology evolves.

"We built Zenlytic to help enterprises get answers they can trust from their own data, with a developer-first approach to keeping business context accurate," said Ryan Janssen, CEO at Zenlytic. "This transaction allows Chord to build on that work, combining our analytics engine with their data infrastructure and activation capabilities so customers can move from asking questions to acting on the answers."

Chord is the analytics harness between AI and company data, helping enterprises across industries scale AI with answers and actions they can trust. Combining data ingestion, AI-powered analytics and activation, Chord works with companies' existing data warehouses to turn natural-language questions into reliable answers and enable agents to act across business channels. The platform maintains business context and governed metrics, applies existing permissions, validates queries, and gives data teams visibility into agent activity. Founded in 2021, Chord is based in New York.
